Rockstar’s UI team explains how the Vice City HUD has evolved, from a phone you hold in the hand to accessibility options built in from the start.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first thing I noticed about GTA 6’s interface was how much it felt like GTA. That sounds obvious, but it's a big design achievement to keep the same series going for 25 years and ensure the UI and HUD feel familiar while still developing new visual quirks.

My first impressions of the HUD from my time reviewing GTA 6 were familiar but evolved just enough: the same icons in the same places, but sharper and more refined, with in-game apps and the character's phone. That’s no accident. Rockstar’s UI team has spent the game’s development working out how to keep the series’ look while making it feel fresh.

“Almost 25 years ago, we helped bring Vice City to life,” says Stuart Petri, Vice President of Art: 2D/UI Design. What began as “a simple visual design language”, he says, has become “far more sophisticated, layered, and considered”.

The team's challenge was to make the UI and HUD “feel fresh, contemporary, and relevant for a new generation, while retaining the heritage that makes it unmistakably GTA”. Petri points to the visual signatures that connect past and present: the iconic Pricedown font, the familiar minimap, the wanted stars and the Wasted screen.

The interface also needs to know when to disappear. “It should be there when you need it, but at the same time is not distracting,” Petri says. “A single press of a button gets you what you need, then back to the game and it’s gone.”

There are plenty of customisation options too, from making the mini-map larger, dynamic, or even adding a top-of-the-screen compass or removing it all. The default UI is balanced and riffs on past GTA games: a small map, subtle police ratings, and small health bars.

His summary is short: “Twenty-five years on, the DNA remains.”

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Sam Grosset, Associate UI Director, UI/UX Design, says the team wants the UI to feel “like a natural extension of the game world, supporting players without interrupting gameplay or breaking immersion, unless necessary to do so”.

The biggest example is the phone. “It was a big shift for our phone interface to be in-hand,” Grosset says, “but it supports that feeling of playing as Jason or Lucia and helps us stay embedded in the world.”

The phone is a tap away, but feels connected to the UI design, layered in humour – BuckMe and RydeMe apps or the Waink app to scan and record the world, all help make GTA very modern and typically Rockstar all at once.

Grosset says accessibility was “considered from the outset”, and that “designing for diverse needs enables us to create better games for everyone”.

In practice, he says, that means options such as “selecting a larger font size, opting for a more minimal screen experience, or making a controls tweak to sprinting”. Rockstar wants every player to have options to play the game how they like, so if you want the classic experience, it's here, but if you want more assists, those are here too. And I don't regret losing the ability to tap a button to run for a second (though bikes still have the old input).

Mark Tennant, Vice President of Animation, says the physical side of the partnership needed “a lot of thought and iteration”. Players can interact with their partner in “a natural, loving way”, with “a believable progression based on their overall investment in the relationship”.

The animators had to find “a realistic balance between player agency and partner response while keeping things fun, passionate, and rewarding”, Tennant says.

All of that sits on top of the everyday stuff. Tennant says there are “close to a thousand animation sets for ambient activities”, plus “hundreds of bespoke one-off events and custom sequences”. Keeping them consistent meant working closely with the design team across the whole world.

You’ll never consciously notice most of it. But when a character can’t open a door without bumping a hip, it’s a sign Rockstar wants you to feel the weight of Leonida.

#9031. GTA VI Player Banned From PlayStation Network for Sharing Photo He Took in the Game

GTA VI Player Banned From PlayStation Network for Sharing Photo He Took in the Game

A Grand Theft Auto VI player says he received a 30-day suspension from PlayStation Network’s social features for sharing a photograph he took in the game.

The player, who uses the name DerrickGott007 on X (formerly Twitter), says he received a notification from PlayStation Safety informing him that his account had been temporarily restricted for violating the platform’s Code of Conduct. The notice cited the sharing of “pornographic or obscene content” as the reason for the suspension.

According to Derrick, the image was captured using GTA VI’s built-in camera feature and showed a nudist resort within the game. The location, which is apparently a nudist colony, is a beachside area near the main protagonist’s house featuring non-player characters who are either fully or partially nude. TweakTown notes that some players have referred to the location as Tiki Touchdown.

Following the suspension, Derrick warned other players about sharing similar images through PlayStation Network messaging, writing: “Do not, I repeat, do not send any photos taken with the in-game camera across the PSN messaging network that contain nudity.”

DO NOT, I REPEAT DO NOT SEND ANY PHOTOS TAKEN WITH THE IN GAME CAMERA , ACROSS THE PSN MESSAGING NETWORK THAT CONTAIN NUDITY. I JUST GOT A 30 DAY PSN SOCIAL FEATURES BAN FOR SENDING MY FRIEND A PHOTO OF THE NUDIST COLONY IN GTA6 THAT I FOUND. https://t.co/vsoIjmpGrt

— DerrickGott007💎 (@derrickgott007) November 20, 2026

Sony’s Community Code of Conduct prohibits users from sharing, requesting, accessing, distributing, or storing “material that is obscene, pornographic, or illegal.” The policy does not appear to distinguish between content created outside a game and images captured from within one. As a result, the player’s actions may fall under the platform’s existing restrictions, despite the image originating from GTA VI itself.

As Engadget points out, the rules are murky. Sony is apparently comfortable selling a game that contains such content to customers, but not with those customers sharing it with friends. At best, it’s inconsistent; at worst, it’s hypocritical.

Derrick says that the 30-day ban not only stops him from messaging his friends but also prevents him from playing multiplayer games such as Call of Duty. If he falls foul of Sony’s rules again, he could face more restrictions.

#9030. Exhibition celebrates Delftware, the Dutch art form that became the ‘Ikea of its day’

Ceramics in Blue Loves You, “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever” Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag

On a tour of ceramics displays in museums across Europe ahead of a landmark new Delftware exhibition she was organising, Suzanne Lambooy realised they all had something in common: they were empty of people. “There was no one there because ceramics can feel cold and distanced,” she says. “They can be hard to bring alive, because the makers are anonymous, and [the objects are] often displayed in glass cases.”

But for Lambooy, ceramics are all about human connection, and she was determined to do something different. The result, Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, opens this month at the Kunstmuseum in The Hague, where she is the curator of decorative arts. It will, she says, be “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever”. Equally importantly, she promises it will be captivating and enjoyable.

“Delftware is so much fun, and we’re going to prove that,” she says. “We want to show the love craftspeople put into these pieces. It has inspired, and it continues to inspire, so many craftmakers—we’ll give them a platform.”

Natasja Sadi's Suikerbloemen (2024) Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag, photo: Studio Roodenburch

Around 1,000 objects, including vases, teapots, plates, wall plaques and tiles, will be on display at the Kunstmuseum, which has one of the largest collections of the art form that is perhaps the best-known cultural export of the Netherlands. Also on show in Blue Loves You will be Delftware-inspired pieces, including the blue dress worn by Queen Máxima of the Netherlands for her husband’s 2013 investiture, its bodice embroidered with Delft-derived flowers. “There’s a lot more to it than blue and white fridge magnets,” Lambooy says.

Although the porcelain is known for its characteristic colouring, the show will include examples of both white and multicoloured Delftware. It will explore its history, dating back to the 17th century. The form was originally a high-end Chinese import, displayed in the wealthiest homes. But when factories started to make their own version of it in Delft, it was transformed.

“It became an on-trend, functional brand that was affordable for every home and on every budget: it was the Ikea of its day,” says Lambooy, whose co-curator for the long-term show is the television presenter Janny van der Heijden (who is also a judge on the country’s version of The Great British Bake Off).

Ceramics in Blue Loves You, “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever” Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag

The quintessential Delftware piece was the tulip pyramid, some of the best examples of which were made for King William III, born in The Hague, and his English wife Queen Mary II, who were the joint monarchs of England, Scotland and Ireland in the late 17th century. “Mary exported Delftware to Britain—she was the most important woman in its history,” Lambooy says.

The porcelain’s connections to Dutch colonialism will also be explored, with exhibits including an installation of sugar flowers by the floral artist Natasja Sadi, whose family are originally from the former Dutch colony of Suriname and whose ancestors were enslaved.

• Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, Kunstmuseum, The Hague, 28 November-31 December 2029

#9029. Cosentino supports architectural creativity with Ēclos mineral surface

Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.

Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.

The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.

This gives Ēclos a premium look, Cosentino explained, and makes it a fitting constituent for the most sophisticated interiors.

According to Cosentino, it is in the junctions and details that a kitchen or room feels resolved and where its architectural character emerges.

“For architects and designers, the section deserves as much consideration as the elevation,” said the company. “The placement of a joint, the treatment of an edge and the relationship between adjoining surfaces shape how a material is perceived.”

“These details establish the architectural language of an element, whether the intention is to suggest a continuous volume or to make its assembly visible.”

Although surfaces are often selected based on their colour or pattern, Cosentino says that full-body design should be just as crucial a consideration, allowing exposed edges and transitions between levels or materials to contribute to building a coherent form.

“With Ēclos, the patterning is constructed within the slab rather than confined to its face,” continued the brand. “That makes the relationship between surface and depth an important part of the design conversation, particularly where edges remain visible.”

“The interest lies not just in the appearance of the material, but in how it can be cut, assembled and brought into a project with adjacent finishes.”

Its fabricators can advise how cutting, profiling, jointing and installation can help a designer’s vision come together.

The process can involve reviewing samples, fabrication drawings and, where appropriate, physical mock-ups.

“The position of a seam or the treatment of an exposed edge can subtly alter the proportions and perceived weight of an element,” said Cosentino.

“The aim is not necessarily to make every joint disappear, but to make each one deliberate.”

“Whether the intention is a continuous volume or a clearly expressed assembly, the junction deserves as much consideration as the surface itself,” the brand continued.

Ēclos launched earlier this year and joins an expanding portfolio of low-silica, high-recycled mineral surface worktops from Cosentino, including Silestone, Dekton and Sensa.

It is suitable for both residential and commercial environments and can be used on worktops, splashbacks, walls and other surfaces.

The first Ēclos collection – Eclectic Veins – incorporates 10 stone-like designs, ranging from ice-white styles to dramatic darks, all made with a minimum of 50 per cent recycled content.

The material is practical for everyday use, withstanding scratches and stains, and is easy to clean and maintain.

It is also resistant to temperatures of up to 220 degrees Celsius, including contact with hot cookware.

To learn more about Cosentino and Ēclos, visit the company’s website.

#9028. Photographer’s Camera Plunges 150 Feet Off a Cliff After Tripod Mishap

Photographer’s Camera Plunges 150 Feet Off a Cliff After Tripod Mishap

A photographer didn’t expect to see her camera again after it plunged 150 feet off a cliff in Arkansas — until a well-known photographer stepped in.

KY3 reports that on November 19, Heinrichs was hiking on Hawksbill Crag in the Upper Buffalo Wilderness.

Hawksbill Crag is a magnet for photographers thanks to the unusual way it juts out over the oak-hickory forest.

Heinrichs was doing just that, taking photos near Hawksbill Crag with her Nikon D750 mounted on a tripod.

“I turned around for maybe five seconds or so and turned back around to my camera and I saw it falling off the side of a cliff,” Heinrichs tells KY3. “About 150 feet down.”

The problem? One of the tripod legs wasn’t locked properly, causing it to fall over. This is normally bad enough without the camera going over a huge cliff.

“It was heartbreaking,” adds Heinrichs. “I could just feel my heart sink and drop when it happened.”

The photographer turned to a local Facebook page, Our Buffalo River, explaining that she “had a camera mishap” and that her D750 was now at the bottom of Hawksbill Crag.

Tim Ernst, a wilderness and nature photographer who is based in northern Arkansas, saw the post and responded.

“Hey, I got an excuse to run out to the Crag,” Ernst tells KY3. “So that was an easy call on my part. I literally jumped up and took off and headed to the Crag.”

And it turns out that Heinrichs is a fan of Ernst, who is a well-established photographer whose work has appeared in National Geographic and the New York Times.

“I’ve followed Tim Ernst for years,” says Heinrichs. “And so for him to be the one to reach out and do that it, I was starstruck a little bit.”

Ernst found the camera sitting on a pile of leaves. However, it wasn’t in great shape.

“I immediately knew it was not good because the lens that was on it had actually separated,” says Ernst.

It appears the camera is beyond repair, but Heinrichs says she’s grateful to Ernst for reaching out and trying. She does plan to replace the camera.

#9026. Melania Trump Is Selling $150 Digital Photos of Herself Taken by Ellen von Unwerth

Melania Trump Is Selling $150 Digital Photos of Herself Taken by Ellen von Unwerth

U.S. first lady Melania Trump is selling digital photos of herself shot by influential fashion photographer Ellen von Unwerth for $150.

Melania made the announcement of the sale of “exclusive” photographs taken by von Unwerth in a post on X (the platform formerly known as Twitter) on Sunday. The launch coincides with the release of MELANIA: The Series, a new two-part production focusing on the wife of President Donald Trump, which debuted on Amazon Prime Video on November 20.

— MELANIA TRUMP (@MELANIATRUMP) November 22, 2026

According to the product listing on Melania’s official website for the “PhotoArchival Digital Edition”, she collaborated with von Unwerth over a two-day photo shoot “to develop the visual narrative” of the images. The photographs are being sold for $150 as a digital album delivered in the form of a movie file.

According to a report by Newsweek, buyers are also required to have a cryptocurrency wallet on the Solana blockchain to store the digital collectible. While customers can currently pay by credit card, they must connect their cryptocurrency wallet to Melania’s website before completing the purchase.

“Melania Trump is launching PhotoArchival Digital Edition, an exclusive collection of digital photographs by internationally acclaimed fashion photographer Ellen von Unwerth,” the announcement on X states. “The collection presents a visual portrait of Mrs. Trump, showcasing von Unwerth’s distinctive artistry. Its release coincides with the debut of MELANIA, The Series, a new two-part production streaming on Amazon Prime Video.”

Von Unwerth also shot the photography for Melania, the documentary about the first lady released in January, and some of the images featured in the $150 PhotoArchival Digital Edition appear to be the same. Another image shows Melania standing beside a mirror in a strapless black dress as someone holds a clapperboard in the shot.

The release of Melania’s digital photo collection follows a recent interview in which von Unwerth, one of the most sought-after fashion photographers working today, claimed that “there’s no money left” in the industry.

#9025. Framery's flexible pod subscription tackles office furniture waste issue

According to office pod brand Framery, when companies resize or move, desks and meeting-room furniture often aren’t deemed “worth the cost of moving” and are discarded during the process.

Framery explained that the EU and US discard 11 million tonnes of furniture a year.

Specifically, the brand points to a study for the European Environmental Bureau, which found that in the EU, 80 to 90 per cent of office furniture is burned or landfilled.

According to the Environmental Protection Agency, in the US, less than one per cent is recycled.

Framery aims to tackle this issue with its office pod subscription service, presenting a more environmentally-friendly alternative to disposing of office furniture when a lease runs out, for example.

“The ‘fast furniture’ trend means 80 per cent of furniture ends up in landfills,” said Framery’s chief design officer, Joonas Vartola. “We wanted to create a pod that’s part of the solution, not the problem.”

“Framery pods are built for heavy use, keeping them in the field for tens of thousands of sessions and out of landfills,” Vartola added.

For example, if there’s an increase in staff and more pods are needed, or if an office’s layout changes.

The scheme covers the full range of its signature line pods, from one-person phone booths to meeting pods.

According to Saija Serpola, managing director and founding partner at IR Partners, using the pods has enabled increased flexibility and reduced financial risk when investing in additional office furniture.

“We can terminate, increase, or change the solution as our organisation develops.”

Framery pods are built from mono-materials, including steel, aluminium, glass and PET.

“Our pods with heavy-duty, high-quality materials engineered to withstand wear and tear,” said Vartola. “It’s all about reducing waste, from design to decades of use.”

As part of the scheme, when a change is required, the pods are dismantled, shipped and rebuilt, rather than discarded into landfill.

According to Framery, each pod is designed for disassembly, with all parts replaceable and recyclable. This includes everything from interior panels, glass, upholstery, carpet, ventilation units and seals.

During refurbishment, each pod is restored to as-new condition and delivered to its next office with a lifetime warranty.

“That is a manufacturing question before it is a commercial one, and it is settled years earlier, on the drawing board.”

#9024. Getty Images Demands Release of Veteran Photographer Detained in Iran

Getty Images Demands Release of Veteran Photographer Detained in Iran

Getty Images is demanding the release of veteran Iranian photojournalist Majid Saeedi, a regular contributor to the photo agency who has been detained in Iran for more than two months.

Saeedi is an internationally recognized photojournalist who has won numerous awards for his coverage of Afghanistan, including a Lucie Award and the Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award. His images have been published in The New York Times, The Washington Post, and Life magazine. Saeedi also received second prize in the 2013 World Press Photo Contest’s Contemporary Issues category.

According to a report by the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), Saeedi was arrested at his home in Tehran on September 9. More than two months after his arrest, Iranian authorities have yet to disclose whether the freelance photojournalist faces any charges or which agency is holding him, despite repeated efforts to obtain this information. Saeedi is believed to be detained in Kerman, a city in southeastern Iran, although his location has not been officially confirmed.

The CPJ and Getty Images have now urged Iranian authorities to release the award-winning photojournalist immediately and unconditionally. They say that the lack of information surrounding his detention has raised serious concerns about his safety, as well as the increasing threats facing independent journalists in Iran.

“Holding Majid Saeedi for more than two months, with no official confirmation of any charges, is unacceptable,” Getty Images VP of Global News Pancho Bernasconi says. “Journalism is not a crime. We join CPJ in demanding Iranian authorities account for Majid’s whereabouts and release him immediately and unconditionally.”

“For more than two months, Majid Saeedi’s family has been left in the dark about his whereabouts, the reason for his detention, and whether he is safe. No journalist should simply disappear into state custody, while Iranian authorities refuse to tell their family what has happened,” CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah says in a further statement. “Majid’s detention is part of a broader campaign to intimidate and silence journalists in Iran — he must be released immediately and unconditionally.

Saeedi has previously been arrested on several occasions in connection with his photographic coverage of politically sensitive events and their aftermath, including in 2009, 2021, and June 2025. According to CPJ, the photographer’s latest detention comes amid an escalating crackdown on independent journalism in Iran, where authorities have increasingly resorted to arrests and lengthy prison sentences to suppress critical reporting.

Previously, PetaPixel reported on two female photographers, prominent photojournalist Yalda Moaiery and 18-year-old artist Shaghayegh Afshar, who were sentenced to a combined 24 years in prison in Iran. Meanwhile Tahmineh Monzavi, an acclaimed Iranian documentary photographer, was sentenced to 74 lashes for documenting an Iranian female singer’s concert.

#9022. Insta360’s X6 Winter Update Syncs 360° Video Capture with the Slopes App

Insta360’s X6 Winter Update Syncs 360° Video Capture with the Slopes App

Insta360 has announced a winter update for the X6 360-degree camera that ties footage to activity data in the popular ski and snowboard app Slopes, linking the footage to GPS data without needing a dedicated GPS accessory.

Slopes is a popular ski and snowboard app that provides digital trail maps for thousands of resorts worldwide. Because it is tied to a smartphone, the app tracks GPS data and provides riders with detailed information about their runs beyond just standard fitness data, such as top speed, average speed, lift versus run times, and more.

The Insta360 X6 now pairs with the Slopes app through the Insta360 app, providing riders with the ability to tie their footage to the data Slopes records. For example, “footage and data help riders review their progress and revisit moments from their season, from a favorite descent to a family ski day,” Insta360 explains.

“Riders can also connect their phone to X6 using the camera’s new Phone GPS Link feature. Once connected, X6 records GPS data with each shot, with no separate import step or dedicated GPS accessory required.”

Because the X6 captures 360-degree video, riders can combine that footage with the additional data provided by Slopes for specific cuts, like terrain or friends, as well as the ability to highlight specific runs.

“AI Director can identify highlights and assemble an edit,” Insta360 explains. “Dedicated skiing and snowboarding templates give riders another quick way to turn the day’s footage into a video they can share. When filming a friend, InstaFrame 2.0 keeps the selected skier or snowboarder in frame and produces a ready-to-share 4K flat video. With supported settings, 360 Video Backup also saves the full 360 degree view, so riders can go back and choose a different angle from the same run.”

The update to the Insta360 app, which allows the X6 to pair with the Slopes app, is free and will be available starting November 24. The integration will require a firmware update to the X6 as well, but that is performed through the app per usual. Slopes also requires a separate subscription.

#9021. From the margins to the mainstream: the growing market for illustration art

Norman Rockwell’s Home on Leave (1945) © Norman Rockwell

The illustration art market began in the 1960s when, according to Roger Reed, a Manhattan-based independent art dealer in this field, works used in children’s storybooks, product advertising and magazine covers “were taken out of their context in publishing and sold just as paintings”. Some six decades later and the apotheosis of that market has arrived with the recent opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, the $1bn creation of film-maker George Lucas (Star Wars and Indiana Jones) devoted to children’s book art, fantasy art, cartoon images, movie posters, film stills and magazine illustrations, as well as works distinguished as fine art by the likes of Paul Cadmus, Diego Rivera and Carrie Mae Weems.

Lucas and fellow filmmaker Steven Spielberg have been some of the largest collectors of the original art created by illustrators for decades, but many others have caught up. Today, the interest in works by Norman Rockwell, N.C. Wyeth, J.C. Leyendecker, Howard Pyle, Maxfield Parrish, Jessie Willcox Smith, John Held Jr and Charles Dana Gibson, among many others, has mushroomed—and in some cases prices have shot up from almost zero to millions of dollars.

“A lot of the work of illustrators was pooh-poohed by the art world, because they were illustrators,” says the New York-based American art dealer Debra Force, “but you don’t hear that so much anymore.”

Certainly, one doesn’t hear that at the major auction houses where works by Rockwell, Parrish, Wyeth and Leyendecker frequently bring the highest prices in American art sales. Norman Rockwell (1894-1978) leads the pack, with his 1951 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover, Saying Grace, fetching $46m at a 2013 Sotheby’s auction and his 1957 oil painting The Rookie (Red Sox Locker Room) sold for $22.5m at a 2014 auction at Christie’s. The 1922 painting Daybreak by Maxfield Parrish(1870-1966) earned $7.6m at a Christie’s sale in 2006, while a 1943 tempera on panel, Portrait of a Farmer, by N.C. Wyeth (1882-1945) brought $5.9m at Sotheby’s in 2018. Football Hero, the 1914 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover by J.C. Leyendecker (1874-1951), brought $4.1m at a Heritage Auctions sale in 2021, and the 1907 painting Captain Keitt by Howard Pyle (1853-1911) for the frontispiece of his novel The Ruby of Kishmoor earned $702,000 at a 2004 sale at Sotheby’s.

“There’s definitely a hierarchy,” says Aviva Lehmann, the deputy chair of fine art at Heritage Auctions, which sold Rockwell’s 1943 work So You Want to See the President! in 2025 to the White House Historical Association for $7.2m.

However, “Rockwell’s success has not been at the expense of these other illustrators”, says Skye Lacerte, an illustration art specialist at Swann Auction Galleries in New York. “Rather, it has helped establish a broader market in which collectors and museums are beginning to take the entire field seriously.” She notes that “immediately recognisable” images from magazine covers and illustrations from famous books like Alice in Wonderland, The Wind in the Willows, or L. Frank Baum’s Oz books are highly sought after, as well as advertising art for “companies like Coca-Cola, TWA and Cadillac because those images have become part of American cultural experience”.

Besides the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, there is the Brandywine River Museum of Art in Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania; the Norman Rockwell Museum in Stockbridge, Massachusetts; the Eric Carle Museum of Picture Book Art in Amherst, Massachusetts; and the National Museum of American Illustration in Newport, Rhode Island. That last museum was founded in 1998 by Judy Goffman Cutler, the owner of Manhattan’s American Illustrators Gallery, who claims to have sold Lucas “hundreds” of original paintings by the top book and magazine illustrators. “I sold him his first Rockwell—it was called Going Out,” she says—a 1933 painting that was used on the cover of the Saturday Evening Post. For reasons of “client confidentiality”, she declines to say how many works in the illustration field she has sold to Lucas, only noting that “I built his collection”.

Other museums that aren’t wholly devoted to illustration or storytelling art also have collections of this type of work, most notably the New Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut and the Delaware Art Museum in Wilmington. The New Britain Museum has almost 1,800 works in its Sanford B.D. Low Illustration Collection, named in honour of the institution’s first director who himself had been an illustrator and invited illustrators he knew to donate works for a collection. They include such artists as Willcox Smith, Everett Raymond Kinstler, Stevan Dohanos, Walter Wick and William Steig.

“Interest in illustration art doesn’t begin and end with Rockwell, and the awareness of illustration art as art is definitely increasing,” says Lisa Williams, head of curatorial affairs at the New Britain Museum.

N.C. Wyeth’s Victory Garden (1943) © N.C. Wyeth

Others agree. “I have no doubt that the collective appreciation for the category will continue to grow thanks to its elevation by these museums,” says Quincie Dixon, head of sale in Christie’s American art department. She adds that “private collectors make up the bulk of this market, but perhaps that will change now that there are museums on both coasts dedicated to the category”.

Specialised museums and collections reflect a growing prominence, but they might also be keeping these works segregated. Goffman Cutler states that it is her “goal to have museums include American illustration art in their American art galleries”, which the occasional museum has done, but not many and not too often.

A spokesperson for the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, notes that the “collection includes art from American artists of many backgrounds, including quite a few who have worked as illustrators, among them Winslow Homer, Childe Hassam, William Glackens, Joseph Leyendecker, Charles Sheeler” and some others. Having worked as illustrators doesn’t mean that their illustration work is what the museum shows, and the Leyendecker is not currently “on view”. Both New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, own paintings by Parrish that are not displayed in their American art galleries, but the Art Institute of Chicago has hung its Rockwell, The Dugout (1948), in one of the Arts of Americas galleries, and the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, has hung Rockwell’s 1943 work Rosie the Riveter (which the museum purchased from a private collector in 2009) next to Charles Willson Peale’s George Washington (around 1780-82) and works by John Singleton Copley and James Peale Sr in its Visions of America galleries. “In the same section of the gallery as Rosie the Riveter,” says a museum spokesperson, “are Susie J. Lee’s Johnny [2013], Kerry James Marshall’s Our Town [1995] and a new commission by artist Teri Greeves.”

It seems the greatest test for illustration art is no longer garnering record prices, but if it can enter—and hold its own within— the art historical canon.

The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art’s new admission and membership fees are tone-deaf and self-defeating

The Star Wars director, appearing at the famed conference for the first time, described the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art as “a temple to the people’s art”

While the swooping building is impressive and easy to navigate, the collection is patchy and the displays are at times “bizarre”

After almost a decade of delays and controversies, George Lucas and Mellody Hobson launch a giant space to house a 40,000-piece collection spanning from comics to Star Wars materials to a Frida Kahlo self-portrait

#9019. TTArtisan’s AF 12mm f/2.8 Is a $489 Ultra-Wide Prime for Full-Frame Cameras

TTArtisan’s AF 12mm f/2.8 Is a $489 Ultra-Wide Prime for Full-Frame Cameras

TTArtisan has unveiled the AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH., a new ultra-wide-angle lens for full-frame Sony and Nikon mirrorless cameras. Better still, it’s very affordable.

TTArtisan says its new lens is built for landscapes, architecture, and night-sky photography, all common applications for ultra-wide lenses. With its f/2.8 aperture, it should work well for astrophotography, though real-world performance will depend on how well it controls optical aberrations. For its part, TTArtisan promises “excellent aberration control” alongside “outstanding resolution,” even when shooting wide open.

The AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. lens has 16 optical elements arranged in 10 groups, including a pair of aspherical elements and three extra-low dispersion (ED) elements. The aperture diaphragm features just six blades, a relatively low count by modern standards, though it should produce distinct sunstars.

Many ultra-wide lenses are big, heavy, and difficult to use with traditional front filters, but the TTArtisan AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. is an exception. It weighs between 336 and 349 grams (11.85 to 12.31 ounces) and measures 72 to 74 millimeters (2.83 to 2.91 inches) long, with the Nikon Z-mount version being slightly heavier and longer than the Sony E-mount variant. The lens accepts common 82mm front filters, which is great news for landscape photographers who want to use circular polarizing and neutral-density filters. Because the front element is bulbous, mounting filters requires an extending filter-thread adapter, though TTArtisan includes one in the box and it adds minimal bulk.

The autofocus-equipped lens focuses as close as 0.18 meters (7.1 inches), making it well suited for emphasizing close-up foreground elements. Given its ultra-wide 122-degree field of view, though, it’s clearly not a macro lens. TTArtisan says the lens uses a high-performance stepping motor and supports eye- and face-detection autofocus modes on compatible cameras.

Speaking of compatibility, TTArtisan says the lens works seamlessly on Nikon Z-mount bodies, while some older Sony E-mount cameras have limited functionality. The Sony a7 III, for example, is fully compatible for photo modes but only partially compatible for video. The original a7 and a7 II also lack full compatibility. TTArtisan notes that autofocus performance may be limited on certain bodies, while firmware updates are in development for others. More compatibility details are available on the company’s website.

The TTArtisan AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. lens is available to preorder now for Nikon Z and Sony E-mount cameras at $489.

Although TTArtisan does not list an L-Mount version for sale, one is referenced on the product page. Since the company already makes several lenses for L-Mount, it is reasonable to expect the AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH. to arrive in that third mount down the road.

#9018. Bennetts Associates revives Victorian hospital for University of Edinburgh

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson

The conversion of a Victorian hospital into facilities for the University of Edinburgh, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film forms part of a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are introduced to the Edinburgh Futures Institute by London-based Bennetts Associates, which involved the revitalisation of the Category A-listed building to create teaching spaces for the university, including a 450-seat auditorium.

Central to the building’s new function was the opening up of the programme to the public, highlighted by the creation of a public square at its front.

“A large part of the project was, of course, rescuing the building,” studio founder Rab Bennetts said.

“Our mission, if you like, was to come back and reopen that main entrance, give it a sense of purpose again, open up the space to the street and make it a public space.”

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be announced on 26 November.

Comprising three reuse projects, RIAS said this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “important conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Edinburgh Futures Institute is the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture and the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by Studio Octopi.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

#9017. Nirvana Fans Raise $94K for Photographer Who Shot ‘Bleach’ Album Cover as She Battles Cancer

Nirvana Fans Raise $94K for Photographer Who Shot ‘Bleach’ Album Cover as She Battles Cancer

Nirvana fans have raised over $94,000 for the photographer who shot the cover of the band’s debut album Bleach, to cover her medical expenses as she enters hospice care.

Tracy Marander, the photographer behind the cover of Bleach and Kurt Cobain’s former girlfriend, has been battling cancer for four years. Last week, Marander’s family announced that the photographer was suspending her cancer treatment and entering hospice care.

Marander’s family launched a GoFundMe campaign to help cover her medical expenses, which has raised $94,101 toward its $100,000 goal at the time of writing. Hundreds of Nirvana fans have accompanied their donations with tributes to the photographer and her contribution to the band’s legacy.

Cobain’s widow Courtney Love also urged her followers to donate to the GoFundMe campaign in support of Marander in an Instagram post, calling the photographer “the unsung hero of Nirvana” who believed in the band’s lead singer “before he believed in himself.” In her post, Love describes the American medical system as “broken” and called on people to give what they could, adding “P.S. Kurt owed Tracy a lot of rent.”

A post shared by Courtney Love Cobain (@courtneylove)

Released in June 1989, Bleach was the debut studio album by Nirvana. Marander shot the iconic photograph that ended up becoming the album cover art during a Nirvana concert at Reko/Muse art gallery in Olympia, Washington, on April 1, 1989. Marander’s image shows the band performing live, with Cobain’s hair falling across his face, alongside guitarist Jason Everman, who did not play on the album despite appearing on its cover.

Lisa Orth, a graphic designer at the local music newspaper The Rocket, inverted the light and dark tones of Marander’s photograph to give it the appearance of a film negative. According to Nirvana: Taking Punk to the Masses by Jacob McMurray, Orth designed the album cover in keeping with the signature aesthetic of the band’s record label Sub Pop, which favored plain backgrounds, bold lettering, and striking photography. The cover also gave rise to Nirvana’s now-famous logo almost by accident, when Orth asked The Rocket’s typesetter Grant Alden to set the band’s name in whatever typeface was already installed on the typesetting machine.

Although Bleach received positive reviews from critics, it failed to enter the charts when it was first released. However, the album became popular when it was internationally reissued in 1992 following the commercial success of Nirvana’s second album Nevermind, released in 1991.

According to Nirvana biographer Michael Azerrad, Marander was Cobain’s first serious romantic partner and inspired him to write the song About a Girl. Their relationship lasted around three years before Cobain ended it in 1990. Marander recalled how Cobain encouraged her to develop her photographic talents, but the demands of working full-time and financially supporting him left her with little time to pursue her own creative interests.

“Near the end, we started fighting more and more,” Marander tells Azerrad in his 1993 book Come as You Are, according to reports. “He wanted me to be artistic, and I didn’t have time to be artistic. I was driving an hour to work and an hour back from work. I was supporting him.”

AI generation comes to Cinema 4D and ZBrush, but artists have an 'off' switch.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Maxon, the company behind some of the best 3D modelling software in the form of ZBrush and Cinema 4D, is making a big move into artificial intelligence, but not in the way you might expect. Aware that many artists remain suspicious of AI tools, it's trying to take an approach that sets it apart from the likes of Adobe.

Today, Maxon's launching a suite of generative tools for 3D work but under a separate, optional subscription plan called Maxon Plus. If you don't want to see the AI generators, you don't have to. It's also introducing Agentic Licences for Cinema 4D and Autograph, designed to let AI assistants tackle the tiresome production tasks while artists remain focused on the creative work.

Speaking about the company's direction, Maxon's CEO Dave McGovern frames AI as a workflow accelerator rather than a replacement for artists. "The best thing about AI is when it becomes an actual assistant to you. I can stay in my artistic zone and do my artwork, and then this thing can do some of the busy work or repetitive, technical aspects".

That philosophy sits at the heart of two major updates being rolled out simultaneously today. The big news for many Cinema 4D users will be the launch of Agentic Licences, available at a more economic price than individual or teams licences.

Maxon already introduced MCP (Model Context Protocol) workflows that allow AI assistants such as Claude to interact with Cinema 4D. According to the company, adoption exceeded expectations.

Released on 30 September, it quickly became "the most widely used feature in Cinema 4D's history in the shortest period of time", Maxon's chief product officer Steve Forde says, and people are using it to "handle the crap tasks that you just got to get done". Its limitation is that MCP requires the artist to dedicate their active session to the AI assistant, so they can't get on with something else in the software in the meantime.

The new Cinema 4D Agentic Licence solves that by providing a separate headless copy of the software with Redshift rendering capabilities, allowing AI-driven tasks to run "in the back office" on another machine while the artist continues working in their primary application. The same concept is being introduced for Autograph, the free After Effects alternative that Maxon launched in April.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

"We call it an ambitious intern," Steve jokes, but the company sees the approach as a force multiplier rather than a substitute for staff. "We think the best value would be for each Cinema 4D artist to have an assistant running with them," Dave adds.

This unlocks a way of working in which an AI agent can be assigned to generate dozens of product variations, prepare scene files, organise projects or nodes or check settings while the artist can continue to animate, model or render.

Alongside agentic workflows, the other big news is the launch of Maxon Plus, a new subscription platform that sits separately from Cinema 4D, ZBrush and Maxon One. Starting at $10/€10 per month, it provides cloud services, collaboration features and generative AI-powered tools that can be used directly in Maxon's existing software or outside it – Maxon Plus users don't necessarily need a Cinema 4D or ZBrush subscription.

Three AI tools are available at launch. Model Generator generates editable 3D base models from text prompts or reference images. Users can generate concept previews, refine their preferred direction, and then generate a model that can be brought into Cinema 4D for further work. The tool is aimed particularly at props, background assets and scene-building workflows.

Initially, the AI generation is provided by Rodin, although there are plans to add more providers, allowing artist to choose which model to use.

Clay Builder for ZBrush creates simple low-polygon base meshes that artists can then subdivide, remesh and sculpt traditionally.

Texture Generator applies new materials and textures to existing 3D models using prompts or image references, while allowing artists to maintain existing UVs if required.

The emphasis across the suite of generators is on providing starting points rather than finished artwork, and Steve says the company has been thinking a lot about how it in integrates with real workflows in different creative disciplines. Model Generator is expected to appeal to artists who primarily work in animation rather than modelling and might normally seek out ready-made models to use.

By contrast, ZBrush artists who are passionate about sculpting have different needs, leading Maxon to focus more heavily on workflows such as texture creation and asset preparation.

But the most exciting part of Maxon Plus for many artists may not actually involve any kind of asset generation. Maxon Review will allow teams and clients to review fully interactive 3D work through a browser, bringing Frame.io-style collaboration to 3D content. They can leave comments directly on specific parts of models and scenes, and feedback can then be viewed natively inside Cinema 4D or ZBrush.

The system preserves not only the comment itself but also the exact camera angle and viewpoint from which the comment was made, making it clear what the person was referring to. This aims to addresses a longstanding problem in 3D production, where review processes remain heavily dependent on meetings, screen sharing and real-time feedback.

"One of the things that we have not seen in the market before is asynchronous review of 3D assets," Steve notes. "People will spend up to 30% of their time in reviews just navigating a model or a scene".

With Cinema 4D on the iPad, Maxon Plus will also offer cloud rendering.

Dave and Steve both previously held senior roles at Adobe, so they're well aware of the mixed reactions to AI advances teased at Adobe Max this month. Maxon's deliberately positioned itself against some of the criticisms levelled at AI elsewhere in the creative software industry, taking advantage of its relatively small size and close relationship with users.

"We do have a complete 'turn all AI off' in our products," Steve notes. "That's a button that we purposely put there. "If you're an existing Maxon customer, and you've decided that none of this AI business is for me, I do not want to be any part of it, that's entirely your prerogative".

"We would never say any of this generation stuff is something that should make an artist money on its own," Dave adds. "It's part of their creative journey, and it's their artistic skills that's going to make one of these individual pieces into a value-added output."

#9015. Upside-down cantilever cracks open timber hotel by BIG

Architecture studio BIG has unveiled a hotel building with a stepped, zigzagging design that will function as a “gateway” to the Siegenthalergut urban district in Thun, Switzerland.

Together with landscape architect August + Margrith Künzel, BIG designed the 13,000-square-metre Nachwachsende Stadt (Growing City) development, which will form a key section of the new district.

Nachwachsende Stadt will be comprised of four timber buildings, which will house two hotels, residences and commercial spaces. It will be located on a prominent site in Thun’s new Siegenthalergut district, close to the future Swiss Football Association headquarters.

The most striking of the four buildings is a timber block with a cantilevered corner volume that will be home to both a three-star and four-star hotel.

The stepped design creates terraces that are mirrored by the upside-down design of the cantilevered volume, forming a central rift that will be glazed to let light into the building,

“The Siegenthalergut site is an opportunity to create more than just a new development,” BIG partner Sören Grünert said.

“It allows Thun to grow without losing its character while also raising its profile on the national stage,” he continued.

“With the future home of the Swiss Football Association right next door, the neighbourhood will become the city’s calling card: a community, a gateway, and a landmark all at once.”

The hotel building will have commercial spaces along the street and a rooftop restaurant. It will be complemented by three residential buildings, which will also be built from timber but have a more traditional gridded design.

BIG used timber to help reduce the buildings’ carbon footprint, designing the development for “future disassembly and reuse” so that it can be adapted over time.

The development will also have green roofs, photovoltaic panels and rainwater retention systems to help it achieve a targeted SNBS Gold standard.

Construction on the Nachwachsende Stadt is expected to start in 2028.

BIG also recently designed a “modular blueprint” for Refugee City in Rwanda and the cloud-like Tirana Fountain Plaza above a public park.

#9014. Pelican Protector 2.0 vs YETI Gobox: Photo Gear Hardcase Throwdown!

Pelican Protector 2.0 vs YETI Gobox: Photo Gear Hardcase Throwdown!

With the release of the new Pelican Protector 2.0 Series and the YETI GoBox system with the KOR Insert, I decided to pit them against each other to see which gear case can take a beating and come out on top. And what better way to do it than to stuff them full of glass and roll them down a hill?

We get to conduct a rugged real-world test, and I get to let out my pent-up aggression—it’s a win-win! Both are new models, and the YETI is a brand-new product entirely, so let’s see how they hold up. Scroll to the bottom to see the full specs.

Pelican is the industry standard for transporting gear, and most of you have probably used one. This is the brand-new updated version of a case you already know, the 1510, now part of their Protector Series. There are a few improvements, though a lot of it looks very similar, if not the same, as the cases I already own.

The one solid improvement is the latches. They’re similar to what I have on my Pelican Air, and I’m glad they’re bringing this to the Protector Series at this size. Alongside the latch, there’s now a button that helps secure it. I’ve had this happen several times: I check a case onto a plane and it comes down the belt with a latch open, or worse, two latches open. The extra button keeps the latch from popping up on its own and requires an intentional force applied by a thumb to release the latch, which is a great addition.

Inside, the Pelican has a new lid organizer system compared to the classic Pelican foam. All the pouches are removable and you can shift them around, which is awesome. It also includes a light you can aim, dim, and change colors on, embedded right in the case, so you’re not fiddling with a headlamp every time you work in the dark.

You probably know YETI for coolers and backpacks, maybe not for cases. This is their contender to the Pelican 1510, and it’s similarly sized, so it’s clear they’re trying to get some skin in the gear cases game.

The design does indeed borrow a lot of familiar elements. There’s a top handle for rolling and wheels that are genuinely very smooth, with much less friction than the Pelican wheels. The latches are nice and big and require a two-part process, which is great for checked transport, and it has rubber seals for water resistance.

The one thing YETI offers that’s different is its packing system, which they call the KOR Insert. It comes with a pump, and the pump sucks the air out of these molds. You place your fragile items in between, close it up, and vacuum it down. The mold becomes rigid, forms around the object, and keeps it from wiggling. It’s ideal for transporting large, fragile items, though less useful for a bunch of small, different things like an assortment of camera accessories.

Aside from the packing system, the YETI looks durable but has more moving parts than the Pelican, which creates more potential for wear and tear, and eventually repair. The material is different too—the Pelican comes matte and feels like it can take a lot of scratches and bumps, while the YETI looks like it’ll scuff a bit more easily. Only one way to find out.

The starting weight of each case is worth flagging. The Pelican’s foam is super light, and everything comes in light. The YETI feels considerably heavier. If I’m packing heavy lenses, that starting weight becomes a problem for checking, since the limit on a lot of these is around 50 pounds or 22 kilograms.

The rolling handles differ too. The Pelican’s is all plastic, included at this size for a while now, and there’s no reason to change it. Minimal moving parts, one solid piece that can bend and take stress and hold up. The YETI uses what you’d see on a regular rolling suitcase: a button and aluminum rods that extend all the way up. Very smooth, but a lot more moving parts, and those are exactly the pieces that bend and break on suitcases. I can see having to replace that well before any plastic part on the Pelican.

To replicate how our luggage and airline agents treat delicate gear, I packed both with glass and went looking for a hill. For the record, the Pelican was loaded with six glass pieces while the YETI had four, and they feel about the same weight, which tells you plenty about the weight difference already.

First up, the Pelican down the hill. After the tumble, it still looked fresh and clean, no scratches I could see, and stickers still on. Inside, one of the flimsiest pieces survived, but the mason jar, which was supposed to be the tougher one, was busted. One out of six isn’t bad.

The YETI GoBox also fared well with the tumble, and all four pieces came out intact.

For a more real-world approach, I tossed both down a flight of stairs, as we are likely to see these things take more hard surface impacts. The Pelican held up well with all five of its remaining glasses surviving. The YETI came through mostly fine, but one piece was busted this time — the fragile stemmed glass. The KOR Insert maintained its shape.

As a bonus, I wanted to see how each handled a single heavy impact at one point, so I took a sledgehammer to them, which was perhaps the most surprising test result. Both cases bounced the hammer back like a trampoline, with no dent or scratch at the point of impact. They passed the smash test with flying colors.

Both cases size up well, and you can fit a lot in either. Pelican is the clear winner for small lenses, accessories, and the bags and pouches, though it can still take a large gear item with the right laser-cut or custom foam insert.

The YETI with KOR Insert is less suited for small items, but the insert does allow for large items with intricate or unusual forms, and can be reused and reshaped for any items that can fit inside of it. Pelican slightly outperforms YETI in terms of ruggedness and repair simplicity, but both stood up to our beatings pretty well. Hopefully, this gives you enough info to choose the right case for you.

#9012. UK government blocks export of 17th-century British landscape painting

English School, A birds-eye view of Llannerch park, Denbighshire, 1662

Department for Digital, Culture, Media & Sport

The UK government has placed an export bar on a 17th-century painting of the Welsh estate Llannerch Park in Denbighshire, northeast Wales, thought to be the earliest known British country-estate landscape painting.

The export ban, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the work, will initially expire on 19 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £550,000 (plus VAT of £11,000), followed by a second deferral period of four months.

The painting, made around 1662 by an unknown artist, gives a bird’s-eye view of the house and Italian-style gardens at Llannerch Park which “contained a series of marvellous watery innovations: pools, fountains, sculpture, cascades and hydraulic surprises all set off by Baroque architecture, staircases and planting”, says Pippa Shirley, a member of the reviewing committee on the export of works of art and objects of cultural interest which advises the government. The fact that the garden is now lost makes the painting more important, she adds in a statement.

The Llannerch Park garden was created by the landowner Mutton Davies following a tour of France and Italy; according to Sotheby’s, which offered the painting in a sale in 2014 in London, Davies also commissioned the landscape painting in the 1660s, and had remained in the family since. The work failed to sell at the 2014 auction, where it was estimated to sell at £400,000-£600,000. A government spokesperson declined to provide further details regarding the painting's ownership. A slightly smaller version of the painting is housed at the Yale Center for British Art in Connecticut.

“If the painting remains in the UK, researchers will be given the opportunity to explore how people and culture were spreading between Wales, England and the European continent in the seventeenth century. It could also reveal new details about how the artistry of country-estate landscapes developed in Britain,” according to the UK Department for Digital, Media, Culture and Sport.

Offered at Sotheby's London for between £3m and £5m, it is the first painting by the Northern Renaissance master to come to the market in decades

#9011. Jimmy Chin’s Jaw-Dropping Photo Shot on iPhone Makes TIME’s Top 100 Photos of 2026

Jimmy Chin’s Jaw-Dropping Photo Shot on iPhone Makes TIME’s Top 100 Photos of 2026

TIME has released its annual Top 100 Photos of the Year feature, celebrating striking images that capture the biggest moments and events of 2026. One of the featured photos was shot by acclaimed photographer and filmmaker Jimmy Chin using the iPhone 18 Pro, marking a milestone for Apple’s latest flagship smartphone and, of course, Chin himself.

Chin, an Academy Award-winning director, National Geographic photographer, and accomplished mountaineer, photographed his longtime climbing partner, Conrad Anker, as part of a new series, What Holds Us. Chin and Anker have climbed together for 25 years, scaling peaks around the world.

“What I was after was that intersection: human ambition in pursuit of awe and wonder, set against a landscape that was here long before us and will be here long after,” Chin explains.

“Out there you are reminded how small you are. That has always put things in perspective for me, and I hope it does for whoever is standing in front of the picture.”

For Chin, who has shot in many extreme and remote locations throughout his career, the smaller and lighter the gear, the better.

“A production puts something between you and the person in front of you — gear, crew, the apparatus of a shoot. Working this way there was no apparatus. It was just the two of us, which is the only condition under which that kind of ease shows up in a frame,” Chin continues.

Using Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro, Chin was able to travel lighter without sacrificing performance or image quality. As his photo above shows, the iPhone 18 Pro more than delivered — a testament to just how far smartphone imaging technology has come. Chin is far from the only photographer or filmmaker to integrate an iPhone into a professional workflow in recent years.

Chin shot 48MP ProRAW photos the iPhone 18 Pro and then stitched multiple shots to create one of his signature panoramas. The final photo is over 300 megapixels and 25,000 pixels wide. There’s no question it holds up extremely well in the large print featured in the What Holds Us exhibit.

Chin’s photos are also part of the What Holds Us exhibition, curated by Kathy Ryan, appearing alongside works by Alex Prager and Jack Davison. After debuting in New York City in September, the exhibition opens in London on December 4, running at Saatchi Yates Gallery through December 13.

#9010. 13 Winners From the The Royal Photographic Society Awards 2026

13 Winners From the The Royal Photographic Society Awards 2026

The Royal Photographic Society (RPS) has announced the recipients of its 2026 Awards, with cinematographer Sir Roger Deakins among this year’s honorees.

Deakins has received the RPS Centenary Medal, the Society’s most prestigious honor. Widely regarded as one of the greatest cinematographers in film history, Deakins has won two Academy Awards for Best Cinematography and five BAFTA Awards in the same category.

British photographer Timon Benson has received the RPS Award for Achievement in the Art of Photography (under 30). At the beginning of his career, Benson was already attracting significant national and international recognition. His work spans documentary photography, choreography, and abstraction, exploring the nature of photography and its relationship with contemporary life.

The RPS Progress Medal in the Science of Photography has been awarded to Professor Marc Levoy, an American computer graphics researcher and Professor Emeritus of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering at Stanford University. Levoy is also a vice president and fellow at Adobe and a Distinguished Engineer at Google.

British photographic artist Mandy Barker is the recipient of The RPS Award for Environmental Responsibility. Barker is internationally recognized for her work documenting marine plastic debris. Working alongside scientists, she uses photography to highlight the scale of plastic pollution in the world’s oceans and its impact on marine life and the wider environment.

Documentary photographer and filmmaker Polly Braden has received the RPS Award for Social Impact. Her long-term collaborative projects explore how people live and work, and their place in society. Her latest project, Against the Tide, produced with The Guardian, followed young people in 17 coastal towns. The project was exhibited at Arnolfini in Bristol and Firstsite in Colchester, and also brought 16 young people to Parliament to give evidence to MPs.

Now in its 148th year, the Royal Photographic Society Awards date back to 1878. The Society describes them as the world’s longest-running photography awards. They recognize achievements across still and moving images, celebrating individuals rather than individual photographs. The awards cover a broad range of disciplines, including moving image, new media, science and imaging, education, publishing, and curation.

Victoria Humphries, CEO of the Royal Photographic Society, says the awards reflect the breadth of the photographic community and the many ways people contribute to the medium.

“The RPS Awards provide an opportunity to recognize and celebrate those who are making a difference, whether through their creativity, innovation, research, education or their contribution to the wider photographic community,” Humphries says.

“As an organization, we believe that photography is for everyone, and these RPS Awards demonstrate that there are so many different ways to engage with, contribute to and shape its future.”

Deakins says he is particularly pleased to be recognized for his still photography, given his career in cinematography.

“I’m very honored to receive this award from the Royal Photographic Society. Although I have been more known for my work in cinematography, still photography has always been a passion and more personal to me. To be recognized by the Royal Photographic Society for my work in stills is amazing and means a great deal to me.”

#9009. You Already Have an Annuity

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.

Withdrawal plans, Roth ladders, and early access.

My friend Sean Mullaney, the FI Tax Guy, recently published an interesting article about the potential downsides of annuities. One of his observations is so simple that I think it's easy to overlook:

Most Americans already have an annuity. It's called Social Security.

Think about what an annuity is trying to accomplish. You give up some control over a pool of money in exchange for a predictable stream of income, often for the rest of your life. Social Security already provides lifetime income, with the added benefit of inflation adjustments.

For a married couple receiving substantial Social Security benefits, that could represent tens of thousands of dollars of annual income that they don't have to generate by selling investments.

Rare 1889 Photo of Historic New York Giants Baseball Team Is Up for Auction

A rare cabinet photograph of the New York Giants, one of early professional baseball’s most significant teams, taken by renowned baseball photographer Joseph Hall in 1889, is up for auction.

One of Major League Baseball’s oldest franchises, the New York Giants rose to prominence in the late 19th century, winning back-to-back championships in 1888 and 1889, before the modern World Series was established in 1903. The team boasted several future Baseball Hall of Famers during this era. Its legacy continues today as the San Francisco Giants, following the franchise’s relocation from New York to California in 1958.

The photograph, which is being offered by auction house Huggins & Scott as part of a sale which runs through December 3, features the New York Giants team that won the 1888 World Championship. The auction house says it has never handled another example of this particular photograph in its imperial cabinet format, making it one of the rarest of Joseph Hall’s baseball team photographs.

Hall photographed many of the Major League baseball teams in 1888 and was widely regarded as the leading baseball photographer of the late 1880s. Hall’s cabinet photographs of professional baseball teams and players are among the most sought-after photographic collectibles of the late 19th century, with his images of teams posing in uniform at ballparks commanding the highest prices.

While a smaller cabinet card featuring the same image of the Giants appeared at auction several years ago, Huggins & Scott says it cannot recall seeing another example of this photograph in this larger format. According to the auction house, the size and quality of the print are particularly noteworthy given the limitations of photographic production in the late 19th century. Producing photographs of this scale and quality required a considerable investment of time and resources, and the auction house suggests that only a small number of prints may have been made.

Unlike other photographs Hall took of the Giants that feature an outdoor stadium background, the image shows 19 members of the team posing together in a studio. Among those pictured are six future Baseball Hall of Famers: Tim Keefe, Roger Connor, Buck Ewing, Jim O’Rourke, John Montgomery Ward, and Mickey Welch.

The photograph is up for sale in the Fall Auction at Huggins & Scott Auctions, which runs through December 3.

#9005. New York Times Prohibits Photographers From Using Photoshop 2027

New York Times Prohibits Photographers From Using Photoshop 2027

The latest version of Adobe Photoshop, Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0), added many AI-powered photo-editing features. Not all photographers are thrilled about the increasingly heavy focus on generative AI inside Photoshop, and photojournalists are taking note, too.

As The Verge reports, The New York Times sent an email to freelance photographers and contributors warning them against using Adobe Photoshop 2027.

The email, which was shared on social media, specifically cites features inside Photoshop that use generative AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.”

The Times‘ worries about Photoshop 28.0.0 are more about a perceived lack of clarity surrounding the application’s photo-editing features than the presence of AI itself. Photoshop has included generative AI in many tools for years, including Generative Remove and Generative Expand. The latest release uses generative AI for even more tasks, such as relighting and restyling photos.

New York Times photojournalists and freelance contributors cannot use generative AI on their photos. In fact, as the publication’s ethics standards outline, all published photos must be accurate depictions of real events. This means no people or objects can be added, rearranged, blurred, distorted, or removed. It also means that cropping must be done carefully so as not to omit any relevant details in a scene. Color can be adjusted, but only minimally and in service of accurately reproducing an event as it happened.

The Times adds that any use of AI, including generative AI, must be clearly disclosed to readers. The organization has long embraced Adobe’s C2PA initiative as it relates to image provenance and metadata, and that is not changing.

What has changed, apparently, is how easy it is for a photographer to inadvertently use a feature inside Adobe Photoshop that relies on generative AI, which will then show up in the metadata. This appears to be the primary concern for The New York Times, as it cannot work with photos that are labeled as AI-edited content.

“It has come to our attention that certain functions in Adobe Photoshop 2027 utilize generative AI in ways that may not be apparent to users of the software. At this time we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using this new version when working on assignment for The Times,” New York Times spokesperson Graham James tells PetaPixel.

To prevent these issues, all contributing photographers must entirely avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignments for The Times—an unprecedented blow to Photoshop’s already wavering reputation among professional photographers. Fortunately, it is possible for users to install previous versions of Photoshop through the Creative Cloud app, although it’s not necessarily straightforward. As of this writing, users can roll back to Photoshop 27.0, but no earlier.

Adobe’s insistence on publicizing its generative AI features, rather than the genuinely good and mostly inoffensive improvements made earlier this month to Adobe Camera Raw and Lightroom, has created quite a stir in the photography community. The Times‘s new policy will certainly not help Adobe’s PR problem with photographers.

PetaPixel reached out to Adobe for comment but did not hear back ahead of publication. This story will be updated with any response.

#9004. Fatbergs, pigeons and Pankhurst: rebranded London Museum opens new £437m home

The London sign mounted on a former awning structure that bridges between the former General Market and Market Annexe at Smithfield Market © Hufton + Crow

The new London Museum based at the historic Smithfield Market in Farringdon—one of the biggest museum developments in the UK capital in recent years—will open to the public this week with exhibits including a “fatberg” from the sewers, the Suffragette Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal and Roman writing tablets.

Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal © London Museum

Based at London Wall near the Barbican Centre until it closed in December 2022, the institution was previously called the Museum of London. The new complex, one of Europe’s largest cultural infrastructure projects, is designed by Stanton Williams and Asif Khan in partnership with the conservation architects Julian Harrap.

The museum caused a stir in 2024 when it unveiled a rebrand centred around the image of a defecating pigeon. Sharon Ament, the museum director, tells The Art Newspaper: “It’s not often a museum brand gets into the news. I think that’s because people saw, in our pigeon, the city and their experience: a place full of contrasts. It’s beautiful, it’s fun, it’s also a bit scruffy! I don’t think there’s a better representation of us than a pigeon.”

The first phase of the London Museum will open in a Victorian part of the Smithfield Market © Secchi Smith

The new museum site will open in two phases: the formerly derelict Victorian General Market dating from the 1880s, home to the permanent galleries, will open on 28 November, while the 1960s Poultry Market, which houses a learning centre, temporary exhibition spaces and on-site interactive collection store, will launch in 2028.

“We are using time as an organising principle, so our major spaces all behave differently with their own emphasis, objects and vibe,” says Ament. The General Market houses the Past Time and Our Time sections, plus Night Time. Past Time spans 2,000 years, telling the story of London via landmark events like the Great Fire in 1666 and the 2012 Olympics.

A chunk of the Whitechapel Fatberg © London Museum

“Stars of the collection” like the Cheapside Hoard of Elizabethan and Jacobean jewels; the medal given to Pankhurst to commemorate her 1912 hunger strike; and a sample of the fatberg—a 250-metre long mass of oil and wet wipes—will also feature in Past Time.

“We have two significant but very contrasting buildings in the Victorian General Market and the listed 1960s Poultry Market, representing different moments in London’s history. We think about them as two of the biggest objects in our collection and they lend themselves to different experiences,” says Ament.

Our Time in the Linbury Hall is a social hub at the heart of London Museum, set across the former trading floor of the General Market. Around its perimeter, a restaurant, shop and show space for families and schools sits alongside 13 large installations exploring the ways Londoners have come together © Hufton + Crow

Asked if the museum is just for Londoners, she says that the city’s residents will discover new stories from the city’s vast history, and be part of telling its story today, while for international visitors, “this is a great first place to start their immersion in London”. The museum has an ambitious visitor figure target of over two million annually.

There are 18 people in the curatorial team but the museum is also supported by an academic advisory panel and “some 100,000 people from London and beyond” who have helped shaped the museum. These include various focus groups, community and school groups, and advisory panels such as the museum’s Access Panel and Family Panel

View into part of London Museum’s "London Tastes" display, exploring the changing appetites of a global food city © Hufton + Crow

The cost of the new museum has risen to £437m in total (the budget was set at £337m in 2019). The Greater London Authority, under mayor Sadiq Khan, has given £95m, while the City of London Corporation is contributing £222m. A range of private foundations and sponsors including Bloomberg Philanthropies, the Goldsmiths’ Foundation, the Linbury Trust and the National Lottery Heritage Fund are also backing the project.

As for running costs, statutory funding comes from the City of London Corporation and the Mayor of London, Ament says.

“We also want to find ways to stand on our own feet more,” she says. “That means support from commercial partnerships and activities, like retail, ticket sales, our ‘fan club’ [the museum’s membership] and venue hire. We’re also leasing spaces, known as the museum ‘Houses’, that sit around the perimeter of the General Market, so now we are landlords as well.” She says the sites are sustainable through the use of solar panels and smart technology.

The Stratford-based museum, opening this month, aims to build on the success of V&A East Storehouse, which has attracted 500,000 visitors since it opened in May last year

The revamped museum, which focuses on the history of the UK capital, will open to the public on 28 November 2026

Galleries on lockdown connect online during coronavirus pandemic using #CollectionsUnited

The proposals include growing commercial opportunities, using technologies to support itineraries and for the museum to be informative about its wider history

"The animation paired with the awkward script gives major direct to DVD energy," one person writes. "I think it's the hair and vibrancy, older movies were a little dimmer and hair was less in your face poofy," someone else writes.

Someone else's reaction is to quote from the franchise itself. "This whole Ice Age thing is starting to get very old – Sid, Ice Age, 2002".
