#8922. Extra Skin? 9 Exercises for A Sagging Neck

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

We’re not in love with the term “turkey neck” — it’s just extra skin.

If you don’t want to learn to love the extra chin you’re in (though we wish you would!), you can perform some exercises that may tighten your neck muscles.

Though some swear these moves work, there’s no research backing them up, and they can’t zap away extra flowy skin.

Instead, they’re more likely to help strengthen the muscles underneath loose neck skin. Unfortunately, skin removal is usually accomplished with more intense methods, like surgery.

However, these popular neck exercises are simple enough for a test drive and may help tone your neck muscles naturally.

Exercise may be possible to tighten up a turkey neck, but it doesn’t eliminate loose skin like surgery or lasers.

Yes. Certain cosmetic products and procedures — especially surgery — improve loose neck skin the best. These include surgical neck lifts, lasers, Botox, and certain neck creams.

Surgery and other cosmetic methods for turkey neck can offer impressive results.

Are you not into cosmetic procedures or surgery? Neck-toning exercises and facial yoga movements may offer some improvement. However, loose skin is generally not tightened naturally.

Loose neck skin is normal (and honestly v common).

Still, these simple moves may result in toned neck muscles. Just be careful so you don’t wind up with an actual pain in the neck. If you can, it’s best to chat with a healthcare professional first.

#8921. london museum opens new home in smithfield’s historic general market

designed by stanton williams with asif khan studio and julian harrap architects, the project brings a former center of trade back into public life, using adaptive reuse to connect london’s architectural heritage with its evolving urban identity.

London Museum opens its new home inside Smithfield’s historic General Market on November 28th, 2026, following a decade-long transformation led by Stanton Williams, collaborating architect Asif Khan Studio and conservation architects Julian Harrap Architects. The project gives the Victorian market a new public role, preserving its historic character while opening the building to exhibitions, cultural events and everyday encounters with London’s history. The opening marks 50 years of London Museum and gives the historic Smithfield market a new lease of life as a place for Londoners to explore the past and present of their city.

Designed by Sir Horace Jones, the architect behind Tower Bridge and Leadenhall Market, the General Market opened in 1883 and operated for more than a century before closing in the 1990s. After decades of disuse, its restoration returns the building to public life, preserving its architectural character and introducing new functions across its expansive interiors. The transformation involves more than 70 trades and brings together heritage craftspeople, including master stonemasons, Welsh blacksmiths and the country’s last heritage coppersmiths.

The architects at Stanton Williams, in collaboration with Asif Khan Studio and Julian Harrap work with the existing features of the building. Original market signs, heritage shopfronts and decorative ironwork remain part of the experience, with the wrought-iron Phoenix columns continuing to support the enormous ceiling. The perimeter of historic shopfronts will accommodate independent organizations, extending the activities of the museum beyond its galleries. A pub and children’s arts charity, A New Direction, are among the first occupants, allowing different forms of public and community activity to coexist within the restored structure.

Sustainability is another significant component of the redevelopment. The project is targeting a BREEAM Outstanding rating, which would place it among the top one percent of buildings worldwide under the certification system. Supported by a loan from the Mayor of London’s Green Finance Fund, the ambition is to combine heritage conservation with the environmental requirements of a contemporary public building.

Real Time, Our Time and Past Time form the three main areas of the museum. Real Time occupies West Poultry Avenue, a former covered street transformed into the main entrance of the building that introduces visitors to contemporary London through animated displays presenting changing urban data, from the city’s populations of pubs and bees to residents’ moods and listening habits.  Fragments of pottery and discarded Victorian clay pipes embedded in the floor introduce traces of earlier everyday life.

At the heart of the General Market, Our Time occupies the former trading floor of the Linbury Hall. It combines large-scale installations with a restaurant, shop and family-oriented show space. Its displays explore how Londoners gather and form communities, bringing together objects such as the Lord Mayor’s State Coach, the former Buckingham Palace switchboard and Syd’s Coffee Stall, an East End institution. The space also incorporates contemporary cultural references, including nightclub and shop signs, alongside a soundscape by electronic musician Scanner and a film by John Ogunmuyiwa exploring London’s crowds, from street celebrations to political demonstrations. The displays consider the ordinary places, sounds and encounters that contribute to the collective identity of the city.

Descending to Roman street level, Past Time presents 2,000 years of London’s urban history through objects, archival material and immersive installations. The collection moves from the city’s earliest inhabitants and Roman settlement to its development as a center of trade, imperial power, protest and contemporary culture. Highlights include the Cheapside Hoard, Roman writing tablets, Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal and objects documenting London’s music, fashion and artistic scenes. A six-meter viewing window offers a direct view of Thameslink trains passing between Farringdon and City Thameslink. Set within the permanent galleries, it brings the city’s transport network into the museum, placing London’s history alongside the infrastructure that keeps it moving today.

London Museum places particular emphasis on the participation of Londoners in shaping its new identity. More than 100,000 people, including schoolchildren, artists, writers, craftspeople and local communities, have contributed to the project. Their involvement extends into the collection, programming and interpretation, with displays incorporating contemporary voices alongside objects from the extensive historical holdings of the museum

This approach is particularly visible in the museum’s changing program, which opens with London Tastes, an exploration of the capital’s food culture led by guest editors Ruby Tandoh and Jonathan Nunn. Running from November 2026 to August 2027, the program traces the city’s culinary identity through its markets, restaurants, independent businesses and neighborhood food traditions. The opening also forms part of a larger redevelopment of the Smithfield and Barbican area. The adjacent Poultry Market is scheduled to open in 2028, adding temporary exhibition spaces, a dedicated learning center and a collection store. The phased development will further expand the museum’s presence within the historic district.

With a reported investment of £437 million and an ambition to welcome around two million visitors annually, the project represents a substantial commitment to cultural infrastructure in central London. Its architectural significance, however, lies less in the scale of the investment than in the decision to work with an existing urban landmark. By bringing the General Market back into public use, London Museum demonstrates how the city’s inherited buildings can accommodate new forms of cultural life while retaining traces of the activities that originally defined them.

#8920. 5 Signs You’re in a One-Sided Friendship, According to Experts

Welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

Most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going. If that balance consistently feels off—not just once or twice, but over the course of weeks or months—it’s hard not to wonder whether something deeper is going on.

You might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation. They call, if at all, only when they’re bored or when it’s convenient. And then there’s the sharper sting of noticing how effortlessly they find time for other people—just not for you (a surprisingly common frustration you can read more about here).

To be fair, life can get in the way—people get busy, schedules clash, and our friends can’t always be as available as we’d like—but that doesn’t make it any less frustrating or stop you from feeling resentful when you’re waiting days for a simple “How are you?” But how do you know if this is a temporary lapse or a more unhealthy one-sided friendship? Here are the biggest red flags therapists want you to watch out for.

Look through your texts and DMs: Are you always the first to send a message? When’s the last time they suggested hanging out? You can also experiment by not reaching out to see how long it takes for them to initiate contact. If weeks (or months) go by without a word, their silence may indicate who’s really holding this connection together.

“At a minimum, a good friend (even a busy one) will periodically check in out of curiosity and interest,” Tiana Leeds, LMFT, a therapist based in Santa Barbara, California, tells SELF. After all, someone who truly cares about you should want to know what’s going on in your life, which is why if they consistently don’t try to get in touch (or only expect you to do so), they may not be genuinely interested in your world.

Venting to your friends is natural—some would even argue it can strengthen your bond. That said, being there for each other is supposed to be a two-way street, Hope Kelaher, LCSW, author of Here to Make Friends: How to Make Friends as an Adult, tells SELF.

If someone unloads their laundry list of problems but doesn’t listen to yours, “they’re likely using you as their on-call therapist,” Kelaher says. This one-directional dynamic could look like a person who constantly complains about their boss but changes the subject whenever you open up about your work-related stress. Or they dominate dinner conversations with their dating disasters, yet they’re “busy,” uninterested, or MIA when you need relationship advice. Over time, investing all your time and energy into people who won’t give back can drain your energy, Leeds says, and leave you feeling neglected by a person who’s supposed to have your back.

Maybe they insist on eating at restaurants near their place, which means you have to travel across town every single time. They only reach out when “better” plans fall through (“Hey, my dinner got canceled. What are you doing tonight?”), making you feel more like an afterthought than a priority. More subtly, perhaps they’re only interested in brief 15-minute coffee chats that fit their schedule instead of a dedicated dinner or movie night.

“In a healthy relationship there should always be a give-and-take,” Kelaher says, meaning both people need to compromise. So it’s disheartening when, again and again, someone you’d do anything for won’t meet you halfway (sometimes literally).

Your friend might be a workaholic or chronically forgetful (which, don’t get us wrong, is still frustrating). But that alone doesn’t mean your bond is one-sided.

Instead, “consider the bigger picture and ask yourself, ‘Is their behavior a reflection of not caring about me, or just a difference in availability and communication style?’” Leeds says. As an example, someone who takes five business days to reply to anyone’s messages may not be singling you out. What’s more telling, though, is if that same person who’s “too swamped” to text you regularly posts Instagram stories of brunches, dinners, and post-work meetups with others in their social circle. Or if your usually punctual friend (who’s known for being reliable) is comfortable canceling plans only with you. These inconsistencies, Kelaher says, suggest that they’re perfectly capable of showing up—just not for you.

Let’s say you mentioned how important it would be to have support at your first 5K race. A friend who truly cares might surprise you at the finish line with flowers, or at the very least shoot over a heartfelt “Good luck!” or “Congrats!” In a one-sided friendship, however, this kind of consideration may be missing entirely. They might downplay your achievement (“Sorry I couldn’t make it, but it was such a short race!”) or forget your big day without a hint of apology.

True friends go the extra mile to celebrate your successes and be there during tough moments. That’s why if someone repeatedly forgets significant events like your birthday, or rarely shows empathy for your challenges (like a scary medical procedure, a high-stakes presentation), they may not be as invested as they should be.

Therapists recommended bringing up your concerns non-confrontationally.

Ideally, their response can give you a glimpse into whether they’re aware of this imbalance and, more importantly, if they’re willing to work on it. That said, you can’t force someone to be a good friend, so if they don’t care enough to show up for you, know that you deserve better. “After all, friendships take work, Leeds says. “But it’s not meant to be done by just one person.”

#8919. Estudio A-G uses colour to update 1960s book-lined house in Mexico City

Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona

Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

Monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home’s original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G, was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for new inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

“The restoration was extremely respectful of the house’s original architecture, but we never wanted the result to feel nostalgic,” Gutiérrez told Dezeen.

“Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely new, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for.”

Completed in February 2026, the design uses colour to achieve the transformation, bringing new energy to the original architecture without competing with it. The studio aimed to have the house be recognisably Mexican without falling into tropes.

“I wanted the house to feel unmistakably Mexican, but without relying on folklore or the usual clichés associated with ‘Mexican interiors’.” he said.

“I was much more interested in expressing that identity through materials, craftsmanship, colour and contemporary Mexican design.”

At the centre of the house, a dark-toned timber structure rises through a series of split levels like a sculptural tree connecting the entrance hall, living room, dining room, study and reading areas before unfolding into a double-height ceiling.

“More than a structural element, it serves as a spatial anchor, establishing continuity throughout the interior and reinforcing the vertical dimension of the house,” Gutiérrez said, explaining that wood acts as a warm, unifying element throughout the house.

The studio restored and reintegrated the original wood flooring, ceiling finishes and structural elements. It also reinstalled most of the original wooden bookshelves that had been dismantled and stored.

“Overall, the intervention focused on restoring the elements that were worth preserving while introducing the necessary contemporary updates to make the house fully functional for the way its new owners live today,” he said.

The studio replaced some window frames and all the glass, updated the lighting and electrical systems and rebuilt the bathrooms and kitchen.

However, one of the most significant interventions were the colour blocks and new materials included in the space.

“Colour plays a central role in the project,” Gutiérrez said, calling out soft blue walls that are a backdrop for deep plum sofas, moss green dining chairs, lilac rugs, green serpentine stone and terracotta-toned marble.

“Rather than acting as decoration, colour is used as an architectural tool to organise space, establish hierarchy, and shape atmosphere.”

He also designed custom furniture that pairs with historic pieces – like Antonio Attolini’s 1969 armchairs – and contemporary Mexican art. Works by Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman and Adriana Silva embed culture into everyday life.

Previously, Estudio A-G designed a rooftop bar as a “matriarchal universe,” complete with crocodile-shaped furniture and shrine-like water, for a boutique hotel in a former Spanish colonial manor house in San Miguel de Allende.

#8918. Nopales Benefits: Why You Might Add Cactus to Your Diet

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Looking at a cactus with its threatening spikes and tough skin, you might not immediately think, “Yep, that’s a thing I could eat.” But guess what? Some forms of cacti are edible, tasty, and quite good for you!

Check out why it might be a good idea to pal around with nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus.

The nopal cactus, also known as the prickly pear or the opuntia, is a shrub-like, flowering cactus native to parts of Mexico, Arizona, the Mediterranean, Australia, and other desert regions. It might be recognized by its multitude of connected pads with flowering blooms. (A pad in bloom looks a little like a flat, green paw.)

Nopales flowers are filled with a viscous, seeded substance often used in jams, jellies, pies, cakes, and other sweets. But the stems, leaves, and entire pad (with spines removed, obvs) are also edible. Traditional Mexican preparations include boiling, grilling, and sautéing.

Science is still examining the possible benefits of nopales, so some touted wellness perks are fairly tentative. Here’s a look at what we know about these desert fruits.

Almost any time you see bright colors in edible fruits, it’s a sign they contain antioxidants. This is def true for Nopales!

Older studies have found that the fruit inside their flowers is rich in antioxidants like ascorbic acid, phenolics, and a mixture of betacyanin and betaxanthin. These compounds help fight inflammation by kicking harmful free radicals out of your cells.

Since they combat inflammation, the antioxidants in prickly pear could improve joint mobility. In a 2020 study, people who drank 3 ounces of prickly pear juice daily for 8 weeks had better range of motion and greater ease with daily activities than a control group who drank a placebo.

Research suggests nopales may help steady blood sugar. A 2014 study found that people with type 2 diabetes who ate nopales with a high-carb breakfast had significantly lower blood sugar and insulin levels compared to those who didn’t. However, this study only included 14 participants.

In 2019, a larger systematic review assessed the fruit’s potential for blood sugar regulation. While it found insufficient evidence to support using nopales to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, the authors noted it might significantly reduce blood glucose levels.

Showing your liver some love might involve adding nopales (or a glass of nopal juice) to your diet. According to research from 2023, this has to do with prickly pear’s effects on triglycerides. By helping reduce triglyceride accumulation, nopales could relieve stress on the liver.

Whether you’ve overdone it on booze or are down with a stomach bug, it’s important to rehydrate with a drink that contains electrolytes. Consider prickly pear juice as your back-on-the-wagon beverage. It’s got potassium, magnesium, and calcium to help rebalance your electrolyte levels.

If you can track down fresh nopales where you live, cooking it yourself is a fun (if somewhat complicated) way to take advantage of its benefits. If not, look for prickly pear products, such as juices, being sure to check for added sugars.

You can also take a supplement. Nopales supplements typically contain 500-650 milligrams (mg) per day.

While a prickly pear smoothie or nopales salad can be a healthy addition to your diet, consuming this cactus fruit may have some less-than-desirable side effects, like:

If you’re new to nopales, take it slow at first to see how your body responds.

Don’t let the “prickly” in prickly pear keep you away from this desert gem. When prepared correctly, nopales are unique, nutritious food. Check ’em out when your fruit basket needs something a little different.

#8917. Yes, Your Feet Age. Dermal Fillers Can Help

Barefoot walks on the beach. A day in their favorite high heels. A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago. These are the goals—big and small—of women undergoing foot filler treatments.

Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not new, though it is gaining in popularity. As early as the 1960s, medical-grade silicone has been used to puff up padding deflated by age, years of wear and tear, and fashionable footwear, especially high heels. All of this puts intense pressure on the balls of the feet—otherwise known as the metatarsals.

Over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates. Fat pad atrophy affects 30% of people over the age of 60. Without that natural cushion, the bones in your feet come into closer contact with the ground, which causes a deep bruise-like pain in the heels or balls of the feet when walking barefoot or standing for long periods.

For some perspective, look at the doughy wonders that are baby feet and compare them to yours. As we age, wear and tear breaks down that plush tissue. And if you put your feet to heavy use, you’ll wear down that cushion quicker. Some of that internal cushioning can be restored—even if just temporarily—with the injection of dermal fillers.

“It’s getting very popular because people are already familiar with it for aesthetic [uses],” says Ben Pearl, DPM, a podiatrist at Arlington Foot and Ankle in Arlington, Virginia. Dr. Pearl specializes in sports medicine and treats endurance athletes looking to restore cushion lost in their feet from pounding the pavement.

Patients don’t have just one choice for injectables, though. Many of the same options available for cosmetic use have also shown promise for feet. There’s hyaluronic acid filler, which adds physical volume and cushioning, and calcium hydroxylapatite, such as Radiesse, which adds firm volume while also promoting new collagen growth. Sometimes human body fat is used as the injectable, known as adipose tissue, a practice that is quickly becoming the preferred method.

“[A fat injection] actually recruits your body to rebuild the fat pad in that area so it has a much longer duration,” says Anne Sharkey, DPM, of Soley Podiatry in Austin. Fat allografts from brands like Liposana and Leneva may last as long as two years, compared to hyaluronic acid fillers, which typically need a touch up in six to nine months.

This type of regenerative medicine is appealing to patients. It’s not a promise that the foot will return to its former glory, but that it will be “as close to normal as possible,” says Dr. Pearl.

Dr. Sharkey and Dr. Pearl have both seen positive results from their patients. Scientific studies corroborate the efficacy of the treatment as well. One small study looking at patients with metatarsal pain found five patients had no more pain six months post-hyaluronic acid injections, and those who still had pain could wear high heels twice as long as they could before the injections. Another study surveying patients who had been injected with body fat reported that their pain improved by more than 70 percent on average, 20 months post injection.

While there are a growing number of cosmetic clinics offering the procedure, Dr. Pearl cautions against allowing just any injector at it. That’s because injecting filler into feet is a more complex procedure than an aesthetic injection. For one, knowing where to inject requires an understanding of the foot’s pressure points. In his own practice, Dr. Pearl uses ultrasound to help determine where to replace the fat to offload the pain. Additionally, Dr. Pearl notes, the skin is much tougher on the feet than the face, making it a more complicated area to inject.

This is one reason why Dr. Sharkey set up her practice to include a nail salon—combining cosmetology and podiatry. Her patients are already familiar with dermal fillers. Within the attached nail salon you can get manicures, pedicures, ingrown nail treatment, toenail reconstruction, or dermal fillers for feet.

Try not to groan, but it depends. The cost of the procedure is influenced by how much filler is injected, and which brand is used. Other factors that affect cost include how your provider bills the procedure, and how much experience they have with dermal filler injections.

For cosmetic use, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons places the average cost of hyaluronic acid filler treatment at $715. They estimate nonhyaluronic acid fillers, including Radiesse, Sculptra, and Liposana to cost $901 on average per treatment. However, the feet will almost certainly require more filler than the face, so you can expect the cost to be higher.

But will insurance cover it? Unlikely. “Even though it isn't technically cosmetic, it may not be considered medically necessary, because these procedures are often considered elective and cosmetic branding has a box drawn around it,” says Mark Welter, chief strategy and growth officer at Welter Healthcare Partners, a healthcare business management firm.

If you’re transparent with your provider about any financial concerns you have, they can work with you to find a middle ground between pain relief and high costs. Dr. Sharkey, for example, will often offer her patients more affordable hyaluronic acid fillers as temporary pain relief until they’re ready to dive into a more expensive fat injection.

If injectables aren’t accessible to you, there are other ways to deal with foot pain. Here are some options, most of which require a low financial investment.

A podiatrist can help walk you through any of these options and come up with a plan to minimize your pain.

#8916. the architecture of waiting: reimagining train stations as places for public life

from libraries and community kitchens to cultural venues and sports facilities, new projects are rethinking how airports and train stations can accommodate public life beyond travel.

Train stations and airports are places where people spend a lot of time, but rarely by choice. Most are designed to keep passengers moving, with waiting areas, stores and services filling the hours between arrival and departure. Some recent projects are taking a different approach, bringing libraries, exhibition spaces, sports facilities, and community services into transport hubs. In Warsaw, Seoul, and Rovereto, stations are being used for things that have little to do with catching a train.

For many people, the station is part of a routine, whether it means passing through on the way to work, waiting for a connection, or meeting someone before heading elsewhere. Despite this constant use, there is little to do there beyond the journey itself. A library, a public reading room, or a space for workshops may seem an unlikely addition to a station, but a number of projects are finding ways to make these uses part of the daily commute.

Historically, railway stations have served as important civic buildings, marking the entrance to a city and bringing together people from different backgrounds. Over time, however, security requirements, commercial development, and the growing scale of transportation networks have shaped them around circulation and passenger services. Waiting is mostly perceived as a waste of time rather than an opportunity to create a different kind of urban experience.

In Warsaw, Poland, a new library inside Kondratowicza metro station offers an alternative perspective. Designed by GK-Atelier, led by Grzegorz Kłoda, Metroteka opened in September 2025 with around 16,000 books across a 150-square-meter space. The library includes separate reading areas for adults and children, shared workspaces, laptop loans, and room for public events. A hydroponic garden, where plants grow without soil or natural sunlight, also introduces an educational element focused on subjects such as sustainability and food production.

A similar approach appears in Shanghai, where X-Lighthouse opened inside the city’s South Railway Station in August 2025. The 400-square-meter reading space offers books on literature, architecture, art, local culture, and travel, alongside a dedicated area for children, giving passengers a place to engage with something other than their departure time.

Other projects take this idea further, treating railway stations as places that can support the needs of the surrounding community, including people who may not use the train at all. In Rovereto, northern Italy, the Station for Transformation initiative thinks of new ways in which underused rooms in the historic railway station can contribute to local life. Developed with the municipality, railway infrastructure operator RFI, and the community group La Foresta, the project builds on spaces that have already been reused for coworking, meetings, and a community kitchen. Activities include cooking classes, cultural events, and initiatives that bring residents together around environmental and social issues.

The wider project aims to turn the station into a public hub focused on climate change, biodiversity, and local heritage, proposing spaces for collaboration, education, and experimentation, including a climate-focused community kitchen and areas where residents, researchers, and local organizations can develop ideas together. The initiative makes use of rooms at the station that would otherwise remain empty. It is an example of how the future of transportation architecture might involve rethinking what already exists, as much as building something new.

A related approach is taking shape across smaller towns in Italy through the Stazioni del Territorio program, promoted by railway group FS Italiane. Completed projects in Popoli Vittorito, Matelica, and Urbisaglia-Sforzacosta in 2024, followed by further stations in 2025, introduce public services into railway buildings and previously unused areas. Depending on the location, these include medical consultations, support from the Italian Red Cross, community services, coworking, and training facilities. The project is particularly relevant in smaller communities, where access to public services can be limited and a railway station may already occupy a central position in local life. At Popoli Vittorito, for example, the station houses medical services and screening activities.

Public life does not have to mean large cultural institutions or permanent community facilities. Sometimes, a smaller intervention can change the way people use a familiar place. In April 2026, Vilnius Railway Station introduced Sun Hall, a 320-square-meter multifunctional venue designed by 2L Architects & Engineers. The flexible interior can host exhibitions, concerts, conferences, and creative gatherings, with curtains allowing the space to be rearranged for different events. Located within the operating station, it offers another reason for residents and visitors to enter the building. The project is also the first step in a wider program to introduce similar cultural spaces at railway stations in other Lithuanian cities.

In Seoul, South Korea, the idea extends into recreation and everyday fitness. The city’s Fun Station initiative transforms underused areas of metro stations into facilities for activities that would normally take place elsewhere. Runner Station, which opened at Yeouinaru station in May 2024, provides lockers, changing rooms, and spaces for stretching, alongside running classes and community programs. Further facilities have followed, including a fitness space at Ttukseom station and a park-golf facility at Meokgol station. The program reflects the particular relationship between these stations and nearby recreational areas, including the Han River parks. In August 2026, the initiative expanded into culture with K-Culture Station, an underground venue between City Hall and Euljiro 1(il)-ga stations, using a previously closed space for exhibitions and immersive cultural experiences.

These projects show that train stations and airports can accommodate activities well beyond their usual functions. Yet adding new functions does not necessarily make a place more public. A cultural venue inside a transport hub may still be accessible only to ticketed passengers, open for a few hours a day, or reserved for visitors who can afford to pay. An airport lounge, for instance, might offer comfortable seating and somewhere to work, but its purpose and access are quite different from those of a public library or community center.

What really matters, then, is who gets to take part. Can someone come in to read a book without having to buy anything? Can local residents visit an exhibition without catching a train? Can people use the space without being expected to spend money or move on? These questions become particularly important when stations are considered part of the public space, rather than facilities serving passengers alone. Their relationship with the surrounding neighborhood depends, in part, on whether they welcome the people who live and work nearby, as well as those passing through.

#8915. Ultimate Guide to 4A Hair: Care Tips, Styles, and Maintenance

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Understanding your hair type is key to achieving healthy, luscious curls. Hair types range from 1 to 4 — straight, wavy, curly, and coily — with type 4 being the curliest. Type 4A hair has a fine texture and loose curl pattern, forming springy coils that need special care to stay healthy and vibrant.

Knowing your hair type helps determine the best hair care routine. Caring for 4A hair is essential, whether you’re dealing with dryness or breakage or want to define your curls.

Let’s dive into the world of 4A hair and discover how to keep those curls popping.

Alright, curl friends, let’s break it down. Hair type falls into four main categories:

Now, Type 4 hair is where things get seriously curly and coily. Within this category, we’ve got subtypes A, B, and C,

which refer to the width and density of your curls.

So, what’s the deal with 4A hair? 4A hair is the queen of the fine, loose curl pattern. It forms tight, springy coils that are like tiny, perfect S-shapes. These curls are less dense than their 4B and 4C cousins, making them more defined and delicate. Think of 4A hair as the Goldilocks of coily hair — not too tight, not too loose, but just right.

Your hair is unique and gorgeous, but it requires a bit of extra TLC to keep it looking its best. Here’s a straightforward guide to keeping your 4A hair moisturized, healthy, and thriving:

4A hair tends to be dry as its coily structure makes it difficult for natural oils to travel down the hair shaft. Keeping it moisturized is essential, so incorporate a good leave-in conditioner into your daily shampooing routine. Use deep conditioning treatments weekly to replenish moisture and strengthen your curls.

Don’t forget scalp care, too! For maximum hydration, look for products with ingredients like shea butter, coconut oil, and glycerin.

4A hair is prone to tangles, so detangle gently to avoid breakage. Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers to work through knots carefully. Start from the ends and work your way up to the roots, and always detangle when your hair is wet and coated with conditioner to provide slip and minimize damage.

Heat styling tools can cause significant damage to 4A hair, leading to dryness, breakage, and loss of curl pattern. Minimize the use of blow dryers, flat irons, and curling wands. If you use heat, always apply a heat protectant spray first to shield your hair from high temperatures.

Pro tip: To maintain the health of your curls, opt for air-drying or styles that don’t require heat.

Protective styles like braids, twists, and buns can help reduce manipulation and minimize breakage. These styles tuck away your ends, protecting them from friction and environmental damage.

Cotton pillowcases cause friction, which leads to frizz and breakage, especially for 4A hair. Switching to satin or silk pillowcases instead helps mai

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

Regular trims are crucial for keeping 4A hair healthy and preventing split ends from traveling up the hair shaft. Aim to trim your hair every 8-12 weeks to remove damaged ends and keep your curls looking fresh and vibrant.

Yes, 4A hair is curly and falls under the coily category. It features tight, springy curls that form an S-shape.

To determine your hair type, look at the curl pattern, texture, and density. 4A hair has a loose curl pattern with fine, springy coils, while 4B and 4C hair have tighter curls. 3C hair is curly but not as tight as Type 4.

Washing once a week or every two weeks is generally sufficient for 4A hair. Overwashing can strip the hair of its natural oils.

Regular trims every 8-12 weeks help keep 4A hair healthy by removing split ends and preventing breakage.

Taking care of your 4A hair isn’t rocket science, but it does need a little know-how and the right tools.

Love those natural curls — keep them hydrated, avoid excessive heat, and give them some nighttime TLC.

#8914. Mason & Fifth's Belsize Park guesthouse was designed to be “domestic and low-impact”

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth

Design studio Holloway Li has collaborated with architecture practice New-works to conceive the interiors of this London apartment hotel, incorporating circular features meant to stand the test of time.

Mason & Fifth guesthouses are composed of fully furnished private apartments where guests have the flexibility of staying anywhere from one night to several months at a time.

The company has three sites across London, with one in Primrose Hill, another in Westbourne Park, and now Belsize Park.

The Belsize Park location occupies Ornan Court, a 19th-century mansion block that once formed part of the Ivy Bank residential estate.

Architecture practice New-works adapted the building for hospitality use, establishing a series of communal spaces at ground level that could serve as a social hub for guests.

At its heart is a large shared kitchen, centred by a chunky tiled breakfast island, followed by a lounge area with intimate groupings of timber-frame chairs and two khaki-coloured sofas, complementing the glossy green fireplace.

Just off this space is a cosy snug that’s been painted a warm ochre hue. It’s separated from the lounge by a custom-made curtain that design studio House of Quinn made from earth-toned fabric offcuts.

Holloway Li is behind the design of the interiors. Instead of doing a through-and-through overhaul, the studio instead aimed to develop a “circular economy aesthetic that felt warm, domestic and low-impact”.

“That ambition aligned with Mason & Fifth’s own sustainability agenda and allowed us to explore how historic buildings like this can be retrofitted in imaginative and progressive ways,” said the studio’s creative director Alex Holloway.

In each of the guesthouse’s 56 apartments, the bedrooms are furnished with demountable wardrobes in lieu of fitted joinery.

The wardrobes are made up of lightweight timber parts fixed together with metal brackets rather than glue so that, if necessary, they can be unassembled, flat packed, and re-built elsewhere.

Holloway Li worked with Marble Collective to create countertops and splashbacks for the apartment kitchens; all are crafted from limestone that’s been rejected from quarries because of inconsistencies.

The top edge of the splashbacks has been left slightly craggy and unfinished, further celebrating the stone’s natural flaws.

Almost all of the walls throughout the guesthouse have been simply rendered with multi-finish plaster, and any surface imperfections have been left on show.

“In many cases, the most sustainable decision is restraint,” explained Holloway Li’s senior designer Carrie Coningsby.

“Drawing on principles akin to kintsugi and spolia, the approach celebrates intervention rather than concealing it, embedding repair into the visual language of the space,” she added, referencing historic practices focused on reuse and repair instead of replacement.

Mason & Fifth Belsize Park was shortlisted in the sustainable interior category of this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Other projects in the running included the winning Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo, which is outfitted with materials salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins, and the London Coffee Factory by Steve Jensen Design, which is structured around a reclaimed timber framework.

#8913. Pucker Up! How to Heal Cracked Lip Corners Fast

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

The first step to healing your cracked lip corners quickly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

It might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates quickly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”

Whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will quickly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

If your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

Remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

You might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

Say goodbye to painful cracked lip corners in about a week with these easy tips:

Talk to a dermatologist for customized care if your lip corners become red, swollen, or more painful after a few days.

#8912. HOFF transforms its madrid flagship with a festive explosion of color by studio wanda

inside its flexible 600 m² flagship on madrid’s velázquez street, hoff merges footwear retail, specialty coffee, and art with a sculpted holiday installation by studio wanda.

mariana rodrigues November 24, 2026 4 min

HOFF opened a 600 m² flagship on Madrid’s Velázquez street, and it turns out they are providing way more than just sneakers. Built by architecture studio El Departamento to shift on demand, the fluid layout brings together a retail showroom, gallery, and café designed for rotating exhibitions, workshops, and community meetups. Its latest transformation arrives just in time for the holidays, as Barcelona-based Studio Wanda steps in with an immersive, custom Christmas installation named ‘Velvet Firebloom’. Conceived as a reflection of HOFF’s ongoing exploration of color, materiality, and creative expression, the intervention turns the flagship into an evolving space for design collaborations and cultural experiences.

The flagship guides visitors through a series of rooms that open into a central gathering hub. It captures the brand‘s vision for a dynamic retail concept where shopping, art installations, food, and cultural events naturally collide, creating a platform for creative expression that steps outside the shoebox. Inside, travertine marble, custom furniture, and theatrical spotlights team up to treat sneakers like fine art.

Titled ‘Velvet Firebloom’, the holiday takeover by Studio Wanda freezes the split-second pop of a firework mid-air, sparing visitors the loud bang while keeping all the visual spectacle. Working under the concept of Explosion de Color, the studio unfolded sharp geometric lines that erupt outward from a single focal point, blooming into sculpted paper planes that animate the entire room with tactile gradients. This rush of folded paper spills straight out toward Madrid’s streets, transforming HOFF’s storefront into an uninterrupted sculpture.

Inside, the chromatic burst weaves naturally through the entrance architecture, winding past the travertine display blocks of The Stage and framing the SNEAKS café. Just past it sits The Gallery, where Moisés Nieto curates contemporary design pieces and art publications.

Beyond the installation, Velázquez 37 operates as a dynamic hub built to bring Madrid’s design community together. Upstairs, The Work-Shop hosts talks, workshops, and dinners around a 20-meter folding table, joined by footwear customization at The Charm Bar and intimate gatherings inside The Attic, uniting retail with cultural discovery under one roof.

#8911. Architects and designers celebrate at Dezeen Awards 2026 party in London

Photography by Iona Wolff and Olivia Chenery

The world’s leading architects and designers from over 40 countries joined to celebrate Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble, announcing this year’s winners at a party in London.

More than 550 guests from countries including Angola, Canada and India, as well as Japan, South Africa and Uruguay, joined Dezeen for the event at the historic Royal Opera House in central London.

Guests were welcomed with a champagne reception provided by exclusive drinks partner Veuve Clicquot as they entered the Grade-II listed Paul Hamlyn Hall at the opera house.

The hall’s glazed interior was illuminated and washed in vivid colours drawn from this year’s awards graphic identity in a show design led by Hingston Studio.

Partygoers enjoyed their drinks set against a textile softwall bar backdrop designed by Stephanie Forsythe and Todd MacAllen for Canadian studio Molo, known for its sculptural space partitions, furniture and lighting made from paper and textile.

Dezeen’s co-CEOs Benedict Hobson and Wai Shin Li opened the evening’s ceremony. They welcomed Dezeen’s founding director and board member Rupinder Bhogal to the stage to lead a tribute to the magazine’s founder, the late Marcus Fairs, in honour of its 20th year.

After guests joined in a toast, Hobson and Li then introduced the evening’s keynote speaker, Norman Foster.

The British architect delivered a speech that explored creative and artificial intelligence within the evolving landscape of global architecture. Drawing on his prolific career, the nonagenarian advocated that meaningful innovation requires challenging the status quo.

Dezeen’s editorial director of special projects Max Fraser and awards and events director Claire Barrett then led the evening’s winner announcements.

First to be announced were the design categories, which saw design project of the year awarded to the V&A East’s wayfinding scheme.

Stockholm-based Simon Skinner and British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori were named as this year’s emerging designer of the year and designer of the year, respectively.

Skinner and Ilori won in this year’s Designers of the Year initiative, which recognises the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.

Interiors project of the year, sponsored by Gaggenau, went to Barcelona-based Raul Sanchez’s renovation of an old sailor’s home. Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was awarded emerging interior designer of the year, with Tokyo-based Keiji Ashizawa taking the award as this year’s established designer. The interiors project categories were also sponsored by Programa and Framery.

Architecture project of the year was awarded to Daichi’s treetop sauna. The architecture project categories were also sponsored by Michelmersh and Sanderson.

The evening’s presentations culminated with Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect Elsa Escobedo jointly winning emerging architect of the year, while world-renowned practitioner Lina Ghotmeh was named architect of the year.

All the winners received a bespoke trophy made from sustainably harvested cork produced by Portuguese manufacturer Corticeira Amorim.

Dezeen Awards winners, VIPs and invited guests continued celebrating into the early hours at an exclusive afterparty sponsored by creative technology studio Made by On at the House of Louie‘s sequestered cocktail hideaway, the Alligator Bar.

All Dezeen Awards 2026 winners were published on Dezeen last Monday evening. Each winner was also featured on a dedicated page on the awards website.

The next edition of Dezeen Awards will open in February 2027. Sign up for the Dezeen Awards newsletter to be the first to hear the latest updates.

#8910. What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a big part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

Some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

For infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

If the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels quickly through the digestive system.

While liver issues can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

While green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

#8909. can le corbusier’s last building be disassembled and shipped?

some 22,000 screws hold together the pavillon le corbusier's prefabricated steel frames in zurich, yet its concrete ramp, staircase, and legacy make relocation near-impossible.

annalise kamegawa November 24, 2026 9 min

The Pavillon Le Corbusier on Lake Zurich is the last completed building by the late French-Swiss architect. Made of glass and steel, it is his only building to have been constructed in this format, and it has a tricky history of ownership, construction, and maintenance. Having been approached by the gallerist Heidi Weber, who went on to represent his non-architectural projects, the project was made possible by her tenacity, his experimentation, and a fifty-year land lease from the city.

After its opening in 1967, the pavilion enjoyed decades on that grassy plot. When the half-century period came to a close, Weber, who had a contract stating that she could take everything that was allowed to be moved, packed up the lighting, art, seating, and tables. In conversation with designboom, Christian Brändle, director of the Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, which now manages the Pavilion, mentions a popular rumor in the city: ‘There was always a bit of a difficult relationship between Heidi Weber and the city,’ he begins, before elaborating on the gossip that claims ‘she tried to dismantle the building, which is technically not really possible because of [the Pavilion’s] ramp and the staircase is made of concrete.’

above and banner shows Pavillon Le Corbusier, 2019, Zürich | image by Umberto Romito & Ivan Šuta, Museum für Gestaltung Zürich/ZHdKPavillon Le Corbusier, 1st floor, 2019, Zürich | image by Umberto Romito & Ivan Šuta, Museum für Gestaltung Zürich/ZHdK

In order to claim the building as part of the dispute, it has been said that she tried to take the Pavillon Le Corbusier apart and bring it with her alongside the other interior furnishings. The idea that this was possible comes from the fact that, as Brändle mentions, ‘basically, the building pretends to be prefabricated. Of course, all the frames were screwed together with around 22,000 screws on the building site… but it would be absolutely impossible to keep it as it is and to unscrew it and to rebuild it in another place.’

Here, in this pavilion, Weber gave the architect permission to experiment. Although it is a kind of house with a kitchen, bunker, and unrealized bedroom, it is ultimately a museum for his ideas. ‘He really assembled almost every idea he had as an architect in the pavilion,’ reflects Brändle on what would be Le Corbusier’s final project. ‘And a real key power of modernism has always been that design and architecture should come out of the machine,’ he says, referencing the popular idea of ‘houses as machines for living,’ or ‘une maison est une machine à habiter,’ in French, from his popular 1923 manifesto, Vers une architecture.

Pavillon Le Corbusier, drawing on enamel based on the lithograph “Os 2” from 1964 on the outside of its revolving door, 2025, Zürich | image by Lucas ZieglerPavillon Le Corbusier, kitchen corner, 2015, Zürich | image by Georg Aerni

Brändle cites the fallout of the First World War and how prefabricated homes became a counterpoint to the overly decorated standards of the time. ‘You would divide your architecture into elements that could be produced somewhere and then you bring it to the building site and assemble it over there.’ He goes on to say that ‘Le Corbusier was, of course, always upfront when it came to innovation,’ and wanted to implement these processes in his architecture, but had passed away before truly realizing the potential of this method. Nevertheless, he got to experiment with some of these techniques in the Pavilion, which becomes evident in the aforementioned thousands of screws and the 226 × 226 × 226 centimeter units used to construct the entire building.

The building opened on July 15, 1967, as the Centre Le Corbusier – Heidi Weber Museum. Brändle, who frequently liaises between the city of Zurich and Weber herself, who is nearly a hundred years old, speaks fondly of her wit and foresight. ‘When she visited an exhibition at the Kunsthaus Zürich, the art museum, in 1957 about Le Corbusier and his oeuvre, she decided that she will devote the rest of her professional life to the spread the ideas of Le Corbusier’s ideas.’ Although it was a grand idea, he was already regarded as a kind of ‘star-chitect’ of the period, making him a tricky man to get hold of.

Brändle recounts her cleverness, saying that she finally got hold of him when a property next to Le Corbusier’s quiet, retreat-like home, Le Cabanon, went up for sale. He remarks that ‘Corbusier was a bit nervous to get a neighbor he wouldn’t like because he was there all day. If he had some clothes, it was just a swimming suit, but nothing else because it was hot and he wanted to paint, sometimes even naked!’ To avoid having new neighbors who could disturb his peace, he went about trying to find a buyer himself. He was connected to Heidi Weber, who had already become a successful gallerist, with the idea that perhaps her clients would be interested in the villa.

In the end, Weber went to visit this Mediterranean property under the guise of helping to find a buyer and instead knocked on the architect’s door and proposed the idea of becoming his future gallerist. Though he was shocked, as he had never sold a painting before, Le Corbusier eventually agreed. Unfortunately, she sold almost none of them. ‘She decided to sell her little car, her Fiat Topolino, and she went back to Paris with all the money she had from selling the car and gave it to Corbusier, pretending she sold everything. And Corbusier was absolutely thrilled and said, well, she is a genius,’ Brändle recounts of the moment that she became one of his biggest advocates in both art and architecture.

‘That the pavilion is the only building that is turned by 45 degrees,’ says Brändle of its orientation relative to all the other homes in the neighborhood that surrounds it. ‘[The other homes] are in parallel to the street. Le Corbusier always wanted to build a house that is like the Parthenon in Athens.’ The building was constructed at an angle, but a compromise had to be made. Although the architect wanted direct access from the street, a winding path had to be built instead. ‘And Heidi was very upset [about this] because she said, you are betraying not only me, but also the ideas of Le Corbusier.’ This, alongside the land dispute and other particularities, adds to the tricky history of the architect’s last structure. Since 2019, the building has been considered the third part of the Zurich Design Museum, with the institution embarking on a major restoration of the space, which involved refinishing its sloped roof.

There is an amusing contradiction in the Pavilion’s history. A building conceived around the principles of prefabrication, assembled from modular elements and thousands of screws, has proved remarkably difficult to move. Despite its appearance as a structure that could be taken apart and reassembled elsewhere, its concrete staircase and ramp firmly anchor it to its original site. The story of Heidi Weber’s dispute with the city adds another layer to this curious history, raising questions about who gets to claim a building and what it means to preserve it. In a way, the Pavilion embodies two competing ideas of architecture: one that embraces movement, experimentation, and the possibility of relocation, and another that understands a building as inseparable from its place. Today, under the care of the Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, it remains on the lakeside plot where it was first conceived. Perhaps its greatest achievement is not that it can be moved, but that it continues to make us question why architecture has to stay put.

#8907. How to Calculate Your Rising and Moon Sign: A Beginner’s Guide

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she says.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is important here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she says it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she says.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina says.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

#8906. learning to move is how we first construct ourselves, and then everything around us

a station worth staying in, a car no longer shaped by its engine, a home that needs no ground beneath it, a night train where arriving late is the point. states of motion asks who gets to move, at what pace, and how design can transform the journey itself.

sofia lekka angelopoulou November 24, 2026 4 min

Sometime in the fifth century B.C., Greek sculptors worked out a way to put motion into something that could not move. Contrapposto, as Renaissance artists would later name it, describes a standing figure resting its weight on a single leg, allowing the hips, shoulders, and torso to tilt in opposing directions. Against the stiff, frontal poses of the Archaic statues that came before it, contrapposto introduced a frozen promise of movement.

In 1968, Bruce Nauman walked it. Hands clasped behind his neck, hips swaying, he carried the pose up and down a narrow wooden corridor in his studio. That single-channel video became the basis for a series he was still making half a century later, shown in 2021 at Punta della Dogana. What stayed with me was the scale: seven projections, each large enough to make a man in a T-shirt and jeans feel monumental, and the flesh-and-blood performers executing the exact instructions he had written at the end of the sixties.

Watching them inhabit those movements in the same room pulled Nauman’s interrogation of the body out of the abstract; you were no longer just observing a study of human nature from a distance, but suddenly conscious of your own weight and footing beside them. Curators Carlos Basualdo and Caroline Bourgeois described his original video as a confrontation with ‘the simple fact of learning to walk as our first real way of constructing ourselves.’ What is true of the body turns out to be true of almost everything built around it. We make ourselves by moving, and then we remake the world to suit the way we move.

Time itself was remade across entire countries to accommodate a new way of moving. Until the 1840s, every British town kept its own hours, read off its own sun: Oxford ran five minutes behind London, Carnforth eleven, Barrow nearly thirteen. Then the trains arrived, and the clocks had to agree. The Great Western Railway switched to ‘railway time’ in November 1840; the Railway Clearing House ordered Greenwich into every station in 1847; and by 1855, roughly 98 percent of British towns had surrendered their local noon. North America began coordinating its schedules only after two trains running on different clocks collided at Valley Falls in 1853, and it took another three decades to settle the matter nationally. Your phone tells the time it does because movement needed everyone to agree, and almost everything built since has been designed to take time out of the journey.

The shorter word for this is speed. French philosopher and urbanist Paul Virilio, who approached the subject through architecture, spent a career arguing that speed is a political arrangement rather than a technical fact. We live less in a democracy, he wrote, than in a dromocracy: the reign of speed. Yet if speed is a political decision, then pace is something that was decided, and anything that was decided can be decided differently. This chapter is an account of the people doing exactly that.

Airports and railway stations are being rebuilt as places with a reason to linger, reversing a century of infrastructure meant only to push crowds through. Inside the vehicle, the engine no longer dictates the form around it, turning the cabin into a room, an idea spilling off the road into campers, floating homes, and habitats untethered from land altogether. Cities are reclaiming lanes from cars and handing them back to pedestrians; trains are running slowly on purpose again; transit is being drawn for bodies it was never meant to hold; and the corridors that highways once severed are being stitched back together for the wildlife that used them first.

The promise in contrapposto is a step that never arrives. Nauman’s contribution was to finally take it, awkwardly, for an hour, discovering in the process a body and a room he had not quite met before. States of Motion looks into that same interval: the uneasy, productive space between deciding to move another way, figuring out how to do it, and experiencing what takes shape when we actually do.
